speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: ARTS, LETTERS AND SCIENCES STATEMENT ON SITE FOR NATIONAL CENTRE FOR PERFORMING ARTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as promised I should like to bring the house up to date regarding the choice of a site for the proposed national centre for the performing arts. Since the last session of parliament there have been a number of developments in this matter. Most of these are on the public record, but I might usefully and shortly review some of the more important matters.
First, Mr. Speaker, the mayor and board of control of the city of Ottawa agreed to recommend that the city make available without charge land between Elgin street and the Rideau canal north of Mackenzie King bridge as a site for the proposed performing arts centre. The national capital commission was directed by the government to report on the suitability of the above site and on others that had been suggested. Supported by the unanimous recommendation of their advisory committee on design, the commission reported in favour of the Elgin street site.
In submitting its report the national capital commission said that it had placed before the architects a number of essential conditions laid down by its design committee to ensure that certain long term principles for the development of the Confederation square area would not be infringed. The architects appointed to design the centre went into these conditions specifically and also into the general adequacy of the site for the needs of the centre as they saw them. After carefully investigating the Elgin street site, the architects had reported that the performing arts centre could be built on that site in a manner which would contribute to the development of the area within the principles of the Parkin plan for the central area of the capital. The government thus had the results of very thorough study of the site and its suitability, as well as a report on other sites.
After receiving the national capital commission report with its recommendation I wrote on behalf of the government on February 17 to the mayor of Ottawa to say
that the government agreed to the construction of the national centre for the performing arts on the site between Elgin street and the canal, provided the city would convey to the federal government a clear title to any city lands required for the project. Should the city require time to establish beyond doubt its ability to meet this request, we asked that a rent free long term lease, renewable in perpetuity, be granted, pending the eventual transfer of title, in order that work on the site might begin without delay. The city council that same evening agreed to a memorandum of understanding which makes it quite clear that the city is to make the site available free of charge and clear of all claims or reservations. The only provisions the city had sought were that the centre would in fact be built on the land, and that the mayor of Ottawa should in future years be ex officio a member of whatever board is set up to be responsible for the centre under the federal government. I have since received a letter from Mayor Whitton informing me of the city's agreement to the memorandum.
Reference has been made to controversy surrounding the subject. There has been no such controversy involving the federal government. Our arrangements have been made entirely with the city of Ottawa, and on a co-operative and cordial basis. We have, of course, been aware of the fact that members of an old and distinguished Ottawa family have raised some question about the course of action taken by the city. We trust that this question will be settled amicably and promptly. It will be evident, however, that the clarification of the city's title to the lands in question is a matter for the city to handle. The project for the construction of the centre for the performing arts on the Elgin street site rests firmly on our definite understanding with the city under which we shall receive a clear title to all the lands required.
The centre will, along with the centres to be established in the provinces as part of the centennial program, be of great importance in the cultural life of Canada. To ensure that it will be of outstanding quality the government is making provision for consultation with the best authorities in Canada on the various performing arts that will make use of the facilities when they are completed. I

Statement on National Arts Centre hope to be able to announce very shortly the composition of committees being established for this purpose.
To derive the greatest value from that consultation, and to ensure that the views of the artistic experts and the architects are brought together effectively and continuously within the relatively short time available for this project, the government has appointed Mr. G. Hamilton Southam as co-ordinator. Mr. Southam is president of the national capital arts alliance which had the original study for the centre made, and has had a long and close association with encouragement of the performing arts in Canada. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, he will be a very successful and efficient administrator and co-ordinator of the project.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CONTINUATION OF WATER SERVICE
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence, and I do so now because time is very important. In accordance with the recommendation made by the Cape Breton county council, will the minister give consideration to extending from February 28 to March 15 the date when the Department of National Defence will cease to pump water through a line to Point Edward naval base that now serves a large number of ratepayers of Cape Breton county, in order to allow time to make other arrangements for a water supply?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR CONTINUATION OF WATER SERVICE
speechtext:
I should like to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his intention to ask me this question. The water line referred to is a 12-inch wood-stave pipe built in 1943 to supply water to the Point Edward naval base. By about 1956 excessive leakage was becoming a problem due to the condition of the line and the number of unauthorized tappings by private individuals. A new steel line with related works was completed in 1960. However, the department continued to pump water under pressure to the old wood-stave line because of the approximately 25 families in Coxheath who had come to depend on this line as a source of supply, although no payment was being made.
Recently formal notice has been served on the department of possible damage claims
Inquiries of the Ministry concerning damage to property allegedly caused by water escaping from this line, and as a result I informed the warden of the municipality of Cape Breton by telegram and letter on February 8 that unless the county of Cape Breton would assume all liability, the department would discontinue water supply effective the 28th of this month. In reply I received a letter from the warden asking that an extension be granted to March 15, 1964, but no undertaking was given that the county would assume liability.
I have today sent a telegram to the warden informing him that we would of course extend the water supply until March 15 if the county will save us harmless from liability.
I should point out that in correspondence which has continued over a considerable period of time, the department has offered to provide water from the new steel line on a metered basis; and should this be acceptable, every assistance will be given to the county in order to furnish adequate outlets.

speechtext: May I say that I am very grateful to the Minister of National Defence, and the previous minister, for their excellent co-operation in this matter.

Mr. Speaker, last night, during the discussion on the validity of the subamendment introduced by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Perron), the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) indicated that I shared his interpretation of the application of our standing orders. At that time, he referred to the existence in our country of two systems of procedure, one under which a statutory principle is first applied and then illustrated by jurisprudence and the other where we proceed by establishing precedents which become law.
Of course, it should be pointed out that the error consists in forgetting that this dual system is the one which governs the application of either civil law in the province of Quebec or common law in the other provinces.
But this is strictly a matter of parliamentary law and the suggestion I respectfully make to the Speaker of the house is that standing orders apply equally to all members.
As far as Beauchesne's volume is concerned, it is of course a book of reference helping the Speaker of the house to make his rulings.
I think only a part of Beauchesne becomes law, if you will, as far as this house is concerned. It is that part which reports the rulings made in the British House of Commons when the rules or regulations of this house do not cover a specific case. Indeed, here is what is provided for in section 1 of the standing orders of the House of Commons:
In all cases not provided for hereafter or by sessional or other orders, the usages and customs of the House of Commons in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland as in force at the time shall be followed so far as they may be applicable to this house.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is clear that when Beauchesne's work reports a precedent on usage in the United Kingdom parliament, it evidently becomes an order in the Canadian House of Commons, unless otherwise provided for in the standing orders.
As far as Beauchesne is concerned, like the hon. member for Lapointe, I hope that the translation of that work will be completed as soon as possible and that French copies will be made available to all hon. members.
Point of Order
As the hon. member for Lafontaine (Mr. Lachance) said yesterday, if Beauchesne is worth translating, it is worth at least one quotation from the Chair. However, I must say that the house is, in the final analysis, master of its own procedure and not bound by Beauchesne up to a certain point since the very rulings of the Chair can be appealed from; so, it is the house which, finally, decides what procedure is to govern it.

In this regard, we know what the order of authorities is: the first one is the legal authority under acts which have been duly passed. Then, there is the authority under the judgments handed down by the judges in the various courts. Then, we have the authority of jurisprudence and, finally, recognized authorities such as Beauchesne, Bourinot, May and other authors who have dealt with these problems for a long time and whose rulings were approved by the house at the time they were made.
While being in the hands of parliament, so to speak, of each hon. member individually, the Speaker can nevertheless stand on precedents approved by parliament following a vote, either a definite vote where yeas and nays are counted, or merely unanimous consent, or even where the matter is not put to a vote.

Last evening the hon. member for Beauce moved an amendment to the amendment reading as follows. I think I should read this subamendment in view of the allegation that there is a difference between the English and French versions. I have read both, and I do not see any difference. It reads:
The house further regrets that this government did not think fit to use the money from the 11 per cent tax on building materials to increase family allowances following the rise in living costs caused by tax increases over the last 20 years.
The question the Chair must decide is, if the subamendment were now agreed to would it be intelligible and consistent with the amendment as a whole? The deputy chairman of committees in his capacity as Acting Speaker last evening, as reported at page 187 of Hansard, said in part:
We have an amendment respecting the repeal of the tax, and a subamendment concerning the use of the tax.
He also stated, as reported at page 188:
On first reading, the subamendment does appear to be inconsistent with the amendment.
I share the view of the Acting Speaker that the amendment and the subamendment as a whole would not be consistent, and in my view the subamendment is in contradiction

with the amendment. Therefore I cannot accept the subamendment as being in order.
There are two important matters I should like to bring to the attention of the house. I would now like to deal with the alleged question of privilege, which in my view is really a point of order, raised by the hon. member for Lapointe, when he made a distinction between two systems of law; that is, the common law, where he says rulings, jurisprudence and precedents are referred to, and the civil law, where regulations are codified. He seems to be under the impression that for these reasons we in the House of Commons should make use of the two systems. Surely such a distinction cannot apply in parliament, for the very reason that parliamentary law is something quite different from the ordinary civil law or common law as recognized and practised in the different provinces.
Parliamentary law as applied in Ottawa, and for that matter also in the capitals of the different provinces, is based on centuries of tradition and precedents which have marked the evolution of parliamentary freedoms from the time the first parliaments were governed under the rule of the divine right of kings to the stage of parliamentary sovereignty which we have now acquired. This system of parliamentary law is therefore based on the usages and customs of the United Kingdom House of Commons, so much so that our first standing order reads as follows:
1. In all cases not provided for hereafter or by sessional or other orders, the usages and customs of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland as in force at the time shall be followed so far as they may be applicable to this house.
The question is asked, what is Beauchesne made of? And the answer is that it is made of our standing orders, made applicable for nearly 100 years to the House of Commons and previously to the parliaments of united Canada and of the maritime provinces, and of citations made up mostly of the decisions of previous Speakers, either here or in the British parliament. In this connection, when both myself and the Acting Speaker referred to Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 203, that is not Beauchesne's quotation; it is a direct quotation extracted from Sir Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice, thirteenth edition, page 285.
We can, of course, refer to the decisions reported in Gcoffrion or in any other provincial commentator, but surely the decisions based on our own rules and our own precedents should prevail unless we want to balkanize our own procedure, which is already complicated enough as it is. Since the hon. member for Lapointe has referred to the procedure followed in the province of

Quebec, it might be of some interest to him if I referred in the present case to the "regle-ments annotes de l'assemblee legislative" of Mr. Louis Philip Geoffrion and quote article 173, which is as follows:

Annotated regulations of the legislative assembly by Louis-Philippe Geoffrion, section 173:
Any amendment must be written in such a way that the motion on which it is proposed should not take a negative form and should remain intelligible, if adopted.

The hon. member will notice that in the present case the rule followed in the province of Quebec is the same one which we follow ourselves and which I have quoted previously, so that the situation is the same in the United Kingdom, in Canada, and in the province of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I wish in the first place to extend my congratulations to the mover and to the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Both have shown that they deserved the confidence reposed in them and I am *convinced that the house appreciated their responsible and restrained speeches. They are a credit to their constituency, and their constituents will have every reason to be proud of having elected such representatives. As for us, their colleagues, we thank them for having clearly brought out the truly democratic and national spirit actuating the government of this country.
Indeed, this government, which has been in power for less than a year, has put before us last week in its speech from the throne a number of projects underlining the fact that it intends to proceed, as it has done up to now, with its liberal and innovating policy in favour of the various ethnic groups which make up the population of our country, with its policies regarding national unity and welfare, in spite of the difficulties and requirements which we are now facing.
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I shall take the opportunity afforded me by the debate on the speech from the throne to tell you, on behalf of the voters of my county of Laval, how much I appreciate these policies, and to what extent their beneficial effects have been felt and are still felt at home. I would without any narrow partisan feeling, like to raise my voice as a citizen of Quebec, who, like the great majority of his fellow citizens, has understood and realized that if the awareness of our maturity opened up new vistas indicating the important part that may and should be played by us in the world,
The Address-Mr. Rochon it also has given us very definite responsibilities, and outlined a policy to which we must remain true, wherever we come from in our great country, whether from the Pacific coast, the west, the prairies, Ontario, Quebec or the maritimes, and which, as the Prime Minister said last week, is a policy of united action and thought for an ever greater and more prosperous Canada, a Canada which should not only affirm itself but also be respected.
When I speak of raising my voice as a Canadian from Quebec, I am coming, Mr. Speaker, to what I consider my duty, which is to express a few ideas now current in that province, which in 1867, agreed to become a partner in the Canadian confederation, an equal partner, who would accept its responsibilities, but who would also want its guaranteed rights to be respected.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, let us remember the speeches made by the fathers of confederation in favour of this pact, more especially those of Sir Georges Etienne Cartier. Let us remember the formal statement which he made in the house, in 1865:
Mr. Speaker-he said-in answer to what was just said by the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Antoine Dorion), I shall only point out to the members of this house that there is no need to get frightened by the misgivings and the predictions of the hon. member. I have stated on my behalf and on behalf of the government that the delegates who will go to England will not accept any decision from the imperial government unless it is one based on the resolutions passed by this house and they will bring back no others. I have given my word of honour about that.
And, Mr. Speaker, apart from guaranteeing the preservation of our language and our faith, those resolutions also guaranteed the French Canadians this: To be considered equal partners who would take part fully, as their English speaking fellow citizens, in the country's economic, social, cultural and political development.
The federal system did much for the emancipation of our country. From a simple colony, we became a nation, each province contributing its share to the greatness and growth of the country. Not more than another province, but as much as the others, Quebec understood the part it had to play. But, unfortunately, Canada was considered far too long as an Anglo-Saxon country, making it necessary for us in Quebec to fight for our survival. For too long, the federal pact, which stipulated that Quebec should be treated as an equal, was disregarded.
For too long, our status as equal partners was ignored, so much so that we felt-and, unfortunately, too often feel even now-we were strangers in our own country. And yet, if someone should feel at home everywhere in this land, is it not those who, in 1813,

The Address-Mr. Rochon checked the advance of Commander Arnold who had been sent by General Washington to take over Canada, those who fought the glorious battle of Chateauguay where Salaberry and his light infantry put an end to the United States' ambitious dream of making a new American state out of Canada.
Fight for one's survival? Those days are over. The province of Quebec has come to realize its strength, and especially the role it must play within the Canadian confederation; the present government, more than any other, has explained that to Quebec and tries by its legislation to unite all men of goodwill.
Mr. Speaker, Quebec does not want to obtrude itself. Quebec understands that if we want to have a great and prosperous Canada, every citizen must work with goodwill toward that unity of action to which I referred a moment ago. Quebec does not want separatism and those extremists' actions which we deplore are not taken by the majority but by a very slight minority. That a peaceful revolution is under way in our province, only the blind would deny it. But let us realize that for the majority that peaceful revolution means only a contribution to the community and to the enrichment of the culture of our common country, Canada.
I share the views of Mr. Brunet, history teacher at the University of Montreal, when he says that we should show more realism and be less emotional in settling the difficulties arising between French and English Canada. And the chances of doing so successfully were perhaps never better than they are today. The high commissioner to London, the Hon. Lionel Chevrier, who was appointed to that high office just a few days ago, stated at a press conference, as soon as he arrived:
-that we should be pleased with the "tremendous awakening" now taking place among French Canadians.
And1 he went on:
It will be most useful for Canada that French Canadians play fully the part that is rightly theirs in a young nation, but one which already ranks among great countries.

Rather than crying out for separatism, why cannot French speaking as well as English speaking Canadians use more moderation in their claims? Why not try to understand one another by a loyal and sincere discussion of their griefs? Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, that confederation cannot survive without the province of Quebec, and outside confederation Quebec could never succeed in overcoming all the difficulties inherent to an independent state. It would be asking for disaster.

As does the majority, I cannot understand the behaviour as well as some of the statements-which I do not dare to qualify here- made by Canadian people praising that harmful theory. It is said and repeated that separatism will never survive in Quebec or in any other part of this country, be it French or English. This is the phenomenon born of the belief that nationalism emanates from sentimentality rather than reality. It is the phenomenon of a group, the clamours of which should be rejected. It is the phenomenon of a group whose only good achievement has been to shake off the stupor of those whose duty it is to stand for Quebec in its rightful place within confederation. In other words, Mr. Speaker, to resume my thoughts, as we live in one of the most beautiful countries in the world, Canada, let us all be real Canadians.

speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to add my congratulations to those of the many previous speakers to the mover and seconder of the address in reply. I am certain all members feel that the contribution of these two hon. members at this time so early in the session has lent a great deal of prestige to it.
I believe that the rapt attention that has been given to the speech from the throne in all parts of Canada, and to the debate that has followed, has been due in part to the media of television, radio and the newspapers. Many more people are becoming aware of the speech from the throne through these media, and the implications it may have in their daily lives. We who have the honour to sit in the house, sir, give careful and critical scrutiny to the speech from the throne, because through our office we are aware of the very many implications that can be contained in even the most simple and vague phraseology that is used in the speech from the throne as well as in explanations given later by the Prime Minister.
The speech this year has been the subject of many adjectives, both pro and con, depending on which side of the house the particular speaker sat. But no one can deny that

it was very short and very vague. No one m this house can deny that the Prime Minister was justified in devoting a great portion of his address to the maintenance of unity and co-operation in this country. I should like to pay particular tribute to him for doing so. I should like also at this time to compliment the speaker who immediately preceded me for the way in which he tried to portray the causes and effects of the trouble in Quebec today.
I feel justified, Mr. Speaker, in assuming that the members of this house and the people of Canada from now on will have little patience with anyone who endeavours to use this critical issue to further cheap political ambitions, rather than displaying the necessary statesmanship that is so vital if confederation is to survive.
The speech from the throne has been termed simple and businesslike. Well, I heard it, and I can vouch for it being simple. When we come to the description "businesslike", however, we in the official opposition are left with grave doubts. We have heard it said that it lays a firm foundation for a quiet, businesslike session. But if the legislation brought down this session is as ill advised, as ill conceived and as ill planned as it was last session, I am confident that the present session, too, will be far from quiet.
Having said this, I feel certain that the present government, like all previous governments in Canada, does wish to promote legislation which will be of benefit to the citizens of this country. I wish to point out to the hon. gentlemen opposite that now, as perhaps never before, they have a golden opportunity to do just that. I should like very much to deal with a variety of subjects, but on this occasion I will confine myself to one main topic, namely transportation. In particular I intend to deal with one phase of transportation, that is freight rates and the effect they have on southwestern Ontario, specifically on the county of Kent.
The one item in the speech from the throne which created the greatest stir in our immediate area was the indication that perhaps this session legislation will be introduced having to do with transportation and that the basis, at least, of the government's proposals will be the report presented by the royal commission on transportation known as the MacPherson commission.
I listened with a great deal of real interest to the representations which were made by the hon. member for Lambton West on behalf of the trucking industry and I am sure, from his remarks, that he is well aware, as I am, of the serious difficulties which are being experienced in this industry in south-

western Ontario. I would certainly lend my support to what the hon. member had to say in his summation of the problems of the trucking industry, and to his contention that the treatment meted out to this industry over the past few years has been far from optimum. It is my hope that legislation will be introduced to remove many of the handicaps under which this industry operates, and to do away with some of the contentious restrictions which seem to work solely in favour of the railroads.
I am particularly concerned about the way in which freight rates are calculated and applied. In the examples I intend to give I shall use as a basis first class freight rates and a weight of 100 pounds in all instances for the sake of easy calculation. I propose to illustrate how unfair these rates are at the present time and how their application is resulting in definite hardship. These rates are in fact discriminatory, and from time to time they are changed in a manner suggesting a day to day effort to patch up and sustain a most unstable vehicle.
In southwestern Ontario we do have ample physical water and rail transportation facilities. We have a climate which is most favourable for year round production. We have a dense population giving us ample labour reserves and ready markets. Yet despite all this the very heart of the area was made a designated area by the present government on account of chronic unemployment.
What is the reason? May I suggest in no uncertain way that we in this area feel that the freight rate scale to which we are subjected is the real culprit. This one factor is throttling the great industrial complex of which I have spoken, and the tempo of the constriction is ever increasing. It is at the present time driving large segments of our industry out of the area, while preventing new industry from entering.
May I emphasize the fact that designation of this area as a distressed area in no way alleviates the problem. Its only effect is to add gross insult to injury. But I will have more to say about that a little later. Why are we concerned about transportation? What is the story? May I be permitted to simplify as far as I can a most complicated subject for the benefit of all hon. members.
I should like to state that much of my information is taken directly from a brief on the subject submitted to the royal commission on transportation by the southwestern Ontario associated chambers of commerce, which deals with the subject in some detail.
I would certainly recommend this document to the attention of all hon. members for study, because it is the most comprehensive analysis of this problem that I have ever
The Address-Mr. Danforth seen. Southwestern Ontario comprises five of the most southerly and westerly counties in the province of Ontario. In each of these-counties there is at least one major manufacturing community. They are London, St. Thomas, Chatham, Sarnia and Windsor. The-area in between is mainly rural. It is intensively cultivated, and produces an annual income from agriculture amounting to more-than $159 million. Because of the nature of the agriculture most of the major canning companies in Canada, together with distilling companies, breweries, cereal manufacturing companies followed by can, bottle and carton manufacturing companies, are located in this area. In addition we are mass producers of automobiles and component parts, petrochemicals, diesel locomotives and other products.
What does this amount to? Our established factories ship annually $1,208,118,000 of goods; they purchase materials costing; $886,105,000, employ 74,755 persons and have annual payrolls of $291,214,000. I wish to place these facts on the record to illustrate^ the magnitude of the question, and the tremendous impact on the economy of the country of any factors interfering with normaL flow of freight to and from the area.
A major problem is, I think, brought about by our location. We are in the interior of Canada, and our difficulties are magnified tremendously because we are subjected to two different methods of rate calculation. Westbound rates from most origins are equal,, while eastbound rates reflect mileage operated. This creates a directly unfavourable freight rate picture for southwestern Ontario,, and it removes any possible advantage due to location.
Perhaps I may be allowed to illustrate this contention using, as I said, examples based on first class freight and units of 100 pounds. Toronto lies approximately 200 miles east of Chatham, Montreal approximately 600 miles east of Chatham. Now, in shipping 100 pounds of freight eastbound to say Halifax, Nova Scotia, by rail, the rate would be around $2.71 from Montreal, $3.59 from Toronto and $4.41 from Chatham. This illustrates that the-further one is from the east coast in miles, the higher the rate; and since Chatham is around 600 miles further from the east coast than Montreal it seems normal to expect that the additional cost would be roughly $1.70-per 100 pounds. But what happens with regard to westbound traffic? Let us use Winnipeg as a western terminal or destination. The freight rate from Montreal to Winnipeg is roughly $5.89 per 100 pounds. Let us see what the rate is from Chatham, which is 600-miles closer to Winnipeg than Montreal. The rate is $5.89, exactly the same. We receive absolutely no benefit even though 600 miles.

The Address-Mr. Danforth nearer the west than Montreal, and it costs us roughly one third more to ship east than any manufacturer in Montreal. What this means, Mr. Speaker, is that industry from our area can move eastward to Toronto or Montreal, receive as a benefit $1 to $1.70 on every 100 pounds they ship first class and be penalized not one cent because they are moving further east, because the rates to the west would be exactly the same as from southwestern Ontario.
One might say, what about water rates; what about trucks? The water rates are certainly somewhat lower, but they are seasonal; and the trucking rates are somewhat lower, but not too much. This is, in the main, because of fixed railway rates, and they tend to follow the same pattern. I hasten to assure the house, Mr. Speaker, that from time to time there have been changes in the rates. There have been horizontal increases in the rates. These are percentage increases in the prevailing rates for the purpose of raising more revenue. But where we have horizontal rates they only tend to aggravate the lot of the long distance shipper because, shipping further, he incurs a greater cost, and any percentage increase puts him more and more at an economic disadvantage and throws the entire picture further out of balance.
We have had government subsidies for particular commodities. In southwestern Ontario we have subsidies on grain, for example. This certainly helps in definite and specific instances, sometimes to a very marked degree, but it has very little effect on the over-all picture. You may say, what about agreed charges? Well, what about agreed charges? Agreed charges are negotiated rates arrived at when-a major industry has agreed to certain, specific conditions laid down by the railway. For example, an industry may be asked to guarantee 85 per cent of its entire freight business; it may be asked to ship only in carload lots. If the industry will meet these conditions it can obtain rates very much more advantageous than the published rates. These are called agreed charges. They are without doubt responsible for some of the industry remaining in our area, but certainly this can be considered as merely a stopgap measure. It certainly discriminates as between industries and companies, and most assuredly creates an even greater disadvantage and handicap for any small industry whose production capacity rules out any possibility of an agreed charge.
Mr. Speaker, we ask the government to introduce in this session measures to rectify the hardships brought about by this ridiculous application of freight rates. We have already had two major industries leave southwestern Ontario; we have had the Ford Motor Com-
[Mr. Danforth.l
pany leave Windsor and the Chrysler Motor Company parts plant leave Chatham. When major industries leave an area, sub-industries and subcontractors follow them. We in this area cannot afford this type of loss. We cannot allow this condition to continue and make this great area barren of industrial development. The time for action is now. The new Minister of Transport has a real opportunity to initiate measures at this time to prevent any further translocation.
It is true that we were named a designated area, and I join in the protestations made by the hon. member for Wellington South against this designation. In my humble opinion, Mr. Speaker-although my reasons for being definitely against this type of action on the part of the government may vary somewhat from those of the hon. member, because I am within a designated area and he is without-a designated area creates an opportunity for industry moving into the area to obtain definite tax concessions. It enables the municipality to obtain certain favours and monetary advantages when putting people to work. But I think we all agree that men who are in business and industry, who are in charge of great factories, are indeed the finest businessmen in Canada. It is my considered opinion that no short term bargains will have any effect on interesting a major industry to enter a designated area. On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, I think a very suspicious eye will be cast on any area which must offer such monetary inducements.
Although this designation has been in effect, in my particular case, for some months, I have been unable to uncover one single instance where any industry has started in the area I represent that can be traced directly to such bribes. On the contrary, sir, we have lost some potential United States subsidiaries because of this designation, and also because of information given to them by published freight rates which not only portray a rigid discriminatory picture, but, because they do not indicate agreed freight rates, do not in fact give the factual picture of the cost of freight transportation.
We seek immediate and complete relief from this unjust and unfair treatment in regard to freight rates. As I have pointed out, we feel that industry in our area is definitely discriminated against and is being placed in an impossible economic position. We are determined that something be done. Mr. Speaker, we do not propose to withdraw from confederation if we do not obtain everything we want, but this raises an interesting fact; because it is strange indeed that if we were to utilize United States transportation from our area west we would indeed be much better off.

I could place on the record various proposals that might form a basis for alleviating this hardship. However, I intend to wait and study the promised legislation. Perhaps either then, or on the estimates of the Minister of Transport, I shall have an adequate opportunity to elaborate.
I suggest very seriously to the government, Mr. Speaker, that if their portrayal of a businesslike approach to this session is anything but another verbal hoax, then here indeed is one instance where such action is merited, and merited now. Let us have no more of this tongue in cheek, weak, timid, ill conceived and ill planned foray on unemployment in our area, as perpetrated unsolicited on us by our area being made a designated area. We neither ask nor desire special treatment or charity. However, we consider we are entitled to the right to receive equal treatment with every other section of Canada which falls under the administration of the federal government. This treatment we fully intend to have with the minimum of delay. We have been tolerant far too long. The price we are asked to pay in southwestern Ontario is leading one of the richest areas in Canada surely to economic catastrophe. The solution now lies within the power of this government. We shall await to see what action they take.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with the others in congratulating the mover and seconder of the throne speech. I feel that this was the most omissive throne speech in Canada's history, and I should like to speak about one of those omissions. I should like to speak on one of the basic social necessities for the welfare of the country, a subject which is so basic that even the Liberals realized its necessity at the time of the election, but on getting into power could see that they would be stepping on the toes of private insurance companies in carrying out those measures even to a degree.
You must by now have realized, Mr. Speaker, that I am speaking of medicare. I should like to quote from a series of assertions which have been made by those opposed to the principle of tax supported universal coverage.
1.	It should be left to private enterprise, since public coverage would remove the enterprise and competition of individuals;
2.	If public funds are utilized, political bureaucracy will be rampant;
3.	Universal tax supported coverage will destroy initiative and ambition;
4.	Standards will be lowered;
5.	Governments should only concern themselves with coverage for the needy;
The Address-Mr. W. D. Howe
6.	Universal tax supported coverage is foreign to our country;
7.	Requiring people to pay under universal coverage is dangerous and there is no confidence in compulsory equalizations;
8.	If all are covered through tax supported funds, languor, decay and discontent will ensue.
All these foregoing statements are taken from statements made in the United States. 134 years ago, in 1830, by opponents of tax supported education for all children within the population. At that time the battle against universal tax supported education was fought as bitterly as is the current battle against universal tax supported coverage for medical care services. Surely we must realize that good health is as essential to the well-being of a country as is the education of its people. So why must this be left to chance, any more than education? We are leaving it to the individual to decide whether he is ill enough to spend the money to go to the doctor, rather than be free to go with no worry as to the expense involved. Is it on this hit or miss basis that we are going to decide the fate of the health of our nation? Is private enterprise to dictate the terms under which we are going to treat our illnesses? Are we going to use human need to serve the financial ends of the insurance companies?
I would have to answer yes to these questions if we had to depend on the Liberal party to do what they themselves have been promising since 1919. Are election promises only vote getters, with no intention on the part of the government of carrying them out? It certainly looks that way, in that both in 1962 and again in 1963 the Liberals promised a government sponsored national health scheme. Yet after two throne speeches, one session of parliament and the commencement of a second one, there has been no mention of medicare.
Under private enterprise insurance we have a levelling action, in that everybody pays equally and only those who are ill get any return. The amount of illness determines the amount of return. But out of this the private insurance company takes its cut. Our proposition is that people pay premiums according to their means, there is no cut retained by anyone because it is government sponsored, the rates are cheaper because it is compulsory and therefore universal, and the amount paid out has only one criterion and that is the severity and frequency of the illness.
It is my contention that not only should all people of all ages be covered, with no exception, but that funds should be designated for prophylaxis. If we can do research to prevent disease we will not have the cost

The Address-Mr. W. D. Howe of treating the disease. Is it not time Canada took its rightful place, with proper funds, in the world of medical research? Also, funds could be provided for medical education which would not only give us more much-needed doctors but likely doctors of a better calibre, because the students could be selected from a wider range than just the sons and daughters of the people wealthy enough to put their children through medical school.
As a member of the medical profession it seems odd to me that the greatest objectors to such a plan are the doctors themselves. Why do they complain and what are they afraid of? It seems that the doctors are concerned about providing adequate and proper medical services for everyone, yet the profession debates the merits of a government sponsored plan at the time it is most needed, and when it indicates some form of cooperation with the government. The medical profession wants the government simply to pay the premiums of those who cannot afford them and put these people in a position of receiving charity. Also the doctors seem to want a plan that is voluntary because for some reason or other it will cause complications if it is compulsory. However, by making it compulsory it ensures universality and also keeps rates at a minimum. The doctors fear that to make it compulsory the rates must be low and the bulk of the cost derived from another source of taxation; and that as the cost drops the demand for service will rise, leading to unnecessary calls by people who are truly "unsick", and that this overdemand will make the over-all cost rise for everyone. Does this mean that the doctors are putting themselves in the position of stating what the people want? Can they judge whether a person is sick or "unsick"? Is it not the duty of a doctor to treat a patient who comes to him for treatment? Whether the cause be functional or organic is of little importance as long as he is relieving the condition from which the person is suffering. This seems to me rather a jumble of incoherent thoughts on the part of the doctors, and if a doctor is truly a man devoted to the treatment of the sick, these ideas are purely irrelevant and the doctor can get back to caring for the ill with the true assurance he will be paid for his work, that his relationship with his patient will remain intact, and that he may devote all his energies to practising medicine without interference from anyone. It has been fairly well proven that anything that is not understood produces fear. A proper study of our program could readily alleviate the situation. With the New Democratic party program there would be no interference with the doctor-patient relationship but rather an improvement because of the removal of the financial barrier. This 
would also remove the need for charity because everyone would be paying according to his means, so that each and every person would actually be paying. Anyone who pays his share is paying equally with everyone else. I firmly believe in the equality of rights of individuals, not in the equality of people. There is no point in saying that everyone is equal, but I do believe each and every person has equal rights. I do not believe that anything affecting health is intended for a limited few or class who can afford it, but is for the benefit of everyone who needs it as determined by physical health alone.
So a proper plan of health insurance must be (1) universal to include everyone; (2) comprehensive to include the various medical and related needs in co-operation with the medical, dental, pharmaceutical and other related professions and, (3) national, with the provincial plans co-ordinated with the nationwide plan.
There are three areas of special need. They are the geographically handicapped, the economically handicapped and the physical and mentally handicapped by reason of age or chronic confirmed disability. Therefore this becomes a most pressing need for those of the population who have not the best medical care available to them at the moment.
Mr. Speaker, I have with me a brief submitted by the United Church of Canada which was presented to the medical services insurance inquiry in Toronto, and it refers to the geographically handicapped as follows:
In a day when Canada's population movement is from the rural to the urban areas it is easy to forget the tens of thousands of our nation's individuals and families who live and work in isolated places. This large segment of our population is to be found in frontier mining, lumbering and farm areas. Indeed, it is not necessary to go outside such a settled section as southern Ontario to locate isolated sections in which medical services are at a minimum or non-existent.
We believe that an adequate medical services plan would seek to provide adequate hospital, medical, nursing and pharmaceutical services for all areas of our province. Provision should be made for night calls, supply during doctors' holidays and emergency situations. Since ambulance service can be very costly in outlying districts, such service should be provided at a basic nominal fee or such charges taken into consideration in the over-all medical costs. We would laud the air ambulance service supported by public funds in the province of Saskatchewan.
The same brief, dealing with the economically handicapped states this:
Not everyone gets a fair share of the national income. The dominion bureau of statistics states that for several months of each calendar year from 6 per cent to 10 per cent of the labour force is unemployed. For those with jobs, the average weekly wage in 1962 was $80.55. A large percentage of families are burdened with mortgages on houses, furnishings, cars, etc.
Among the economically handicapped, there are urgent and largely unmet health services needs.

though some individuals and families in this group who receive assistance or relief often benefit from free medical services. Still, in the lower income groups, many who try to pay their way are burdened with medical bills. A large proportion endure illness because they cannot pay for medical services. Others find it impossible to purchase prescribed drugs. It is recognized that many doctors have given a great deal of service for which they knew they would never be paid.
The urgent need in this general situation to provide better health services can be underscored by a variety of illustrations. Two will suffice.
There is the bumt-out worker who at the age of 60 years is headed for a scrap heap. At the time of his economic weakness, his need for medical care is likely to be at a high level. He has no insurance. He is short of money. He is ten years from the old age pension requirement-and pension provisions for this category of worker are not uniform throughout Canada. He does not want to beg. He dare not steal. Society must provide an answer to this man and his family because, by his labours as a low income and likely an unskilled worker, he has undergirt our way of life by many years of hard work in mill, mine, factory at sea, in the lumber camps, on big scale construction.
Again, there is the plight of the non-union person and his family. Of these there are many thousands, indeed a million or two who never had a fringe benefit. They have no medical card-no guarantee of health services. They are penalized because they never achieved bargaining power, but their health services needs are many and acute.
Then dealing with the physically handicapped by reason of age, the brief states:
The plight of the chronically ill demands attention now. The need to provide relatively inexpensive bed care for the many older people who do not need much medical attention is an urgent one. There are signs of progress, but the kind of provision required cannot be made available short of a national health service.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to read the actual resolutions contained in this brief, and they date back to resolutions passed by the general council at various meetings in various places since 1952. They are:
(a)	The fifteenth general council, Hamilton, Ontario, September 1952:
Be it resolved that this council expresses its considered opinion regarding national health insurance, as follows:
(1)	Commend the federal, provincial and municipal governments concerned for progress made to date in providing more adequate health services, increasing the number of hospital beds and in related ways improving defective diagnostic, remedial and other forms of medical and surgical care and treatment.
(2)	Recognize the contribution that has been made by certain organizations and agencies that have promoted voluntary health and hospitalization plans.
(3)	Urge all responsible governmental authorities in co-operation with the medical, dental, nursing and related professions to move as quickly as possible to the establishment of an integrated and contributory national health plan.
(b)	The sixteenth general council, Sackville, New Brunswick, September 1954:
The resolution quoted above, passed at Hamilton in 1952, was reaffirmed at this general council meeting at Sackville in 1954.
(c)	The nineteenth general council, Edmonton, Alberta, September 1960:
The Address-Mr. W. D. Howe
Whereas the cost of medical care and treatment is a heavy burden which many are unable to bear; and
Whereas there are those who are deterred from seeking medical care and treatment because of the high cost involved; and
Whereas existing medical insurance plans are inadequate to cover all medical needs; and
Whereas the sixteenth general council has endorsed 'an integrated and contributory national health insurance program':
It is recommended that this general council:
(1)	Re-endorse the principle of a national health insurance plan.
(2)	Commend the province of Saskatchewan for steps being taken to implement such a program on the provincial level; and
(3)	urge the federal government in co-operation with the medical, dental, nursing, pharmaceutical and related professions to establish a comprehensive national health insurance program.
Recognizing the fine work done by the Saskatchewan government in bringing about a partial plan, we must now look at the inadequacies of some of the other provincial proposals. In Ontario we have bill 163, brought down by the Tories, and I would like to read some of the comments on it, again by one of the ministers of the United Church in his capacity as assistant secretary to the board of evangelism and social service of the United Church of Canada; and I quote:
First, we have recent evidence that the members and adherents of the United Church in Ontario solidly support the contention of the general council that a medical insurance plan should be universal, comprehensive and contributory. A systematic, random sample indicates that our people, furthermore, believe such a plan should be government operated and tax supported. We are now conducting a national survey of the United Church, and returns to date show that 67 per cent of members and adherents in Ontario favour a plan having these characteristics. By direct inference, Mr. Chairman, the United Church rejects the limited coverage proposed in bill 163.
So we can see from this that medical care is not only a social necessity and a government responsibility, but it is also the wish of the people of Canada. Continuing the quote:
Second, we stress the fact that the need for a universal comprehensive and tax supported medical care plan is becoming increasingly and critically urgent. Thousands of workers are retiring earlier, for the most part involuntarily, due to obsolescence of their skills and trades in our rapidly changing technological society. The trend towards automation and concentration in merchandising and service industries is steadily reducing the opportunities for self-employment which formerly served to augment the shrinking income of older workers. A few years ago, displaced farm and factory workers often could find work in stores, laundries, construction and other unskilled labouring jobs. These openings are shrinking rapidly in relation to the increasing work force.
We are also told by analysts that the teen age component of the labour force will double by 1970. Already unemployment among youths aged 16-24 is twice as great as the rate in general. The heavy burden of supporting them rests upon working class families at the very time when family allowances and insurance coverage under contract and voluntary plans run out-

The Address-Mr. W. D. Howe
I am convinced, and my church is convinced, that the provisions for medical services proposed in bill 163 are totally inadequate to meet the needs of modem industrial society. This is "horse and buggy" legislation for an urgent space-age need.
One of the greatest fears our government has is facing up to the private insurance companies. These companies charge large premiums to unsuspecting people who feel they are getting protection for when they are ill. Time goes by; then illness strikes, and they find that this illness is excluded or if it is not excluded this time it will be next time around. What kind of security is this to offer a person who can ill afford the premiums he is asked to pay in the first place, and who then finds that he is not protected anyway?
I have had many patients in my office who thought they were protected and found they were not. I recall that a man came into my office on one occasion and told me he had a certain kind of insurance, about which I made a rather caustic comment at the time, and was much embarrassed to find that the man was a salesman for this particular insurance company about which I had made the caustic comment. He assured me I need have no fear that the company would not pay. However, on sending the bill to the insurance company that he represented it was rejected and the man had to pay me himself.
Incidents like this may seem humorous, but this is the only type of protection that the Canadian people have with regard to their health. Just imagine, it is the only protection they have in something as basic and fundamental as health. If it were anything else I am sure something would have been done about it, but when it comes to sick people there is no government support. The attitude is to let them work it out for themselves.
I say to hon. members, therefore, that it is time, far past the time as a matter of fact, for our country to have a government sponsored national health plan. Let us try to rise above medieval mediocrity and give our people a well deserved security and freedom from the staggering expense of an unforeseen medical tragedy.
So, Mr. Speaker, it is readily seen that national insurance coverage will not increase the total social cost but merely distribute it equitably throughout society. The public is not forever deceived. The basic principle in question is not total cost but public as against private administration of the measures required to meet the common man's need for health care. It is within the capacity of government alone to undertake such a vast and unprofitable scheme in co-operation 
with the health professions. Furthermore, this is the duty of government in a society dedicated to the welfare of all its citizens.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I, after my colleagues who took part in this debate, not as a matter of usage, but because they highly deserve it, pay tribute to the hon. members for Longueuil (Mr. Cote) and for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Bas-ford) for the way they discharged their important task. The voices of Longueuil and of Vancouver-Burrard will find long lasting echoes, not only in this house, but all across the nation, if all Canadians want to listen attentively and intelligently.
May I also offer my congratulations and best wishes of success to the new ministers and to those who have assumed new responsibilities in the administration of our country.
I would be unforgiveable if I did not draw the attention of the house to our great loss caused by the departure of the Hon. Lionel Chevrier and the Hon. Azellus Denis. Those veterans in politics, while going elsewhere, surely deserve our deepest gratitude and the assurance of an imperishable memory.
To the former, I wish to express here the gratitude of the hon. members from Quebec who benefited, not only by his leadership, but by his untiring efforts and his sincere adhesion to the cause we are defending and for which he fought with so much love and conviction. Mr. Chevrier has already dedicated half of his life to the service of his country and his people, and his whole life should serve, for French Canadians and the whole Canadian nation, as the example of a man who, at all times, in every region, fought fiercely for respect of the rights of minorities. As for the former postmaster general, he is one of those who do not boast about their highest achievements, but his good humour, his good-fellowship, added to his numerous talents, were a precious asset in this house, and by his brief passage at the head of the Post Office Department he gave it new impetus and stimulus which will be profitable to his successors.
I should also like to extend a warm welcome to this house to the new members for Laurier (Mr. Leblanc) and St. Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) and wish them a fruitful political career.
Mr. Speaker, we are entering upon the second part of the twenty sixth parliament which will give the government an opportunity, with the co-operation of the house, to offer to the Canadian nation the second instalment of its program set out for the duration of one parliament, in the interest of all Canadian citizens. Our legislators will have to

face positively and resolutely the very important and no less serious problems facing our country at this time and the main items, I think, are unemployment, control of our economy and the no less crucial problem of relations between the two main ethnic groups, or national unity.
In those three fields, this government has already taken some positive action-legislative, administrative, and political-which, to date, have had most encouraging results, and the prospects of our economy for 1964 are very promising. On the other hand, the welcome given throughout the country to Mr. Laurendeau and Mr. Dunton, co-chairmen of the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism, gives us good reason to expect results which will bring about the adjustments needed for a greater mutual understanding and a truly equal partnership of our two groups.
In my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I shall briefly -and certainly incompletely-deal with the question of national unity before going on to a subject infrequently discussed in the house, the influence of television on our population, and more particularly on our young people, and concluding by a rapid review of the needs of the Gaspe peninsula and of Bona-venture in particular.
Ever since confederation, not to say for the last two centuries, the two main ethnical groups have faced each other in the same fields as today. A rapid review of Canadian history, since the capitulations of Quebec and Montreal, will certainly confirm it. The stubborn struggle waged by our forefathers to preserve their most precious heritage, their language and their faith, and the exercising [DOT]of their lawful rights as equal partners, is a good illustration of their determination in this respect. History again will teach us that the aim pursued by French speaking Canadians was not, and is not, to dominate or to subjugate the majority, their English speaking fellow citizens, but only to preserve the valuable heritage of their forefathers and the unequivocal right of exercising their lawful rights on an equal standing with their English speaking countrymen.
Canada as we know it today, Mr. Speaker, whose growing economic, social and political emancipation develops an ever-increasing independence, has been built, developed and strengthened thanks to the hard work, the perseverance and diligence of the two main ethnical groups, one English speaking and the other French speaking, each contributing its talents, its intelligence and even its capital-joined in that by many other citizens of different ethnical origins-to make Canada what it is today.
The Address-Mr. Bechard
Mr. Speaker, the ideal of any true Canadian citizen is to work continuously for the development of Canada in all fields, by contributing to its progress not only on the economic level but also on the cultural, political and social levels, by means of his work, his culture, his own knowledge and skills, in whatever part of the country he may be or to whatever race and creed he may belong. However, this should not be understood as being, for the various ethnic groups, the abandonment of their natural development in the Canadian nation, with their traditions, their language and their faith. However, it must be admitted that since 1867, French Canadians, perhaps through their own fault, feel frustrated on account of the rather limited part they play in our country's government. No wonder that, following the economic awakening which has been going on in Quebec since 1960, and in the atmosphere of freedom which prevails in the province, we should witness, on the part of the people of Quebec, a new awareness, which is typical of an adult nation, better informed and better prepared, anxious to really play its part in confederation and to share to a greater degree in the development of our country, and which, to that end, claims its rightful part, as provided in the very constitution of our country. The French Canadian people, to which I am proud to belong, wish nothing more than to participate in the economic expansion of Canada as well as in its intellectual, political and social development, working side by side with their English speaking fellow citizens, as equal partners, that is enjoying the same rights and advantages in the conduct of the business of the nation. No need to get all excited and cry for help. Above all, there is no need to accuse those Canadians of being separatists and wanting to destroy confederation.
Those who advocate separatism, and they are few in numbers, as the solution to the crisis we are now going through do not reflect the general opinion of the people of Quebec. Instead of being alarmed, we ought to welcome this new attitude, this new awareness, because it is proof of a greater maturity and of the burning desire of a people to play a greater and more efficient role in the management of the affairs of its country, something which can only be of value and benefit to the Canadian nation as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, it is to be deplored, however, that this awareness should be accompanied with thoughtless acts on the part of extremists who, more irresponsible than they are guilty, indulge in deeds of terrorism which we strongly reject and condemn.
By the same token, we condemn those who give free and indecent publicity to those

The Address-Mr. Bechard incidents and to those responsible for them, which makes us really wonder. In fact, these extremist disturbances which are stirred up, fostered, fed and kept constantly aroused by certain advertising media and some irresponsible demagogues with their speeches of a revolutionary nature, are not in the best interest of the French Canadian cause. It is not by stirring up extremist tendencies among our Anglo-Saxon friends, by our thoughtless words and actions, that we shall succeed in achieving that harmony we are all hoping for among our two ethnic groups. However, bilingualism has come a long way and the attitude shown by a majority of our Anglo-Saxon friends portends a better understanding among our two main racial groups.
Nothing positive will be done to strengthen national unity by laughing at the Lauren-deau-Dunton commission and by accusing of undermining national unity those who, by popular request, set up that commission, nor will it be by using, for purely electoral purposes, the fear which our English speaking friends understandably feel on account of those extremist happenings in Quebec, which is what a quite important member of this house is doing. On the contrary, such talk does nothing but make matters worse, interfere with the dialogue that is essential in the circumstances and strain relations between the two groups.
That matter of national unity is too important for the survival of our two main ethnic groups and, consequently, of our country to be made the subject of petty political partisanship.
All French and English speaking Canadians must unite. We who represent in this house the two main ethnic groups and who are responsible for the fate and future of our country, let us co-operate and use our intelligence, our skills and all our energies in order to draw our bonds closer, so that both groups will actually enjoy full equality of rights within confederation. The future of our country, our future and the future of our children are at stake.
Under the circumstances, let us get the Canadian people used to the idea of a distinctive national flag and a national anthem which are sorely needed in this country as symbols which would unite Canadians of all origins in affliction as well as in joy. We are an adult nation; let us prove it by adopting a truly Canadian flag. Any delay in this regard can only serve the cause of those who are opposed to it on both sides.
To my English speaking friends, as well as to other ethnical groups, I say that French Canadians do not ask for any preferential treatment or for any special rights. They


merely ask for their rights to be recognized and their legitimate ambitions to be respected, as they are entitled to as one of the two founding races of this country, so as to be able to play their part, fully and efficiently, in the building of a greater, a stronger, a more powerful and a richer Canada. French Canada, more precisely the province of Quebec, does not want to separate itself from the rest of the country, it does not want to leave confederation, for it knows that such a stand would bring disaster not only for Quebec or for French Canada, but for the rest of this country as well.
It wants to stay in Canada and increase the contribution of its culture, its language and all its talents in participating as equal partners with its Anglo-Saxon brothers to the expansion and development of the country. Do try to understand us and, above all, do not be tempted to judge the people of Quebec by the unfortunate acts of terrorism which Quebec disapproves and deplores just as much as you do.
Try and imagine what would be your own reaction to what I would call the flagrant acts of injustice to which the French Canadians have been and, unfortunately are still too often being subjected, in the civil service of their own country, in crown corporations etc.; if you had no access to the senior positions or if you could not be understood when you spoke your own language to such and such civil servant whom you paid with your own taxes.
I am very optimistic about the result of the work undertaken by the present government to promote greater understanding between both ethnic groups, and about the intelligent and useful work of all our leaders and those who have some responsibility in our society, at whatever level it may be.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a word on a matter which very few people want to tackle, so sacrosanct it seems to be; I mean the influence of television on our people, especially our youth. While the press fully reports love tragedies of all sorts, murders, suicides, hold-ups, burglaries, etc., while the civil and religious authorities and our law courts are alarmed at the ever-increasing number of juvenile offenders, this perfect medium of publicity, television, presents in every Canadian home shows where crime, passion, gangsterim and immorality prevail. Guns, revolvers and daggers are used at the drop of a hat to settle the simplest problem seemingly insoluble.
Most movies and a great number of plays shown on television are immoral, even amoral, or at least colourless, and of a disconcerting

foolishness and barrenness. Why must almost every T.V. show feature two or three murders or suicides or depict dissolute living or disgraceful scenes between married people? People wonder after why so many crimes of all types, so many acts of terrorism, are committed within our society, and about the increase in juvenile delinquency, and so on.
How could it be otherwise when such goings on are shown freely to everyone, young and old? The sponsors of such T.V. programs could surely make a much better contribution to the education of our people. It seems to me that T.V. can be more useful to the community. Imagine the responsibility of those who directly or indirectly contribute to the corruption of our youth and those who tolerate such conditions.
I therefore ask the government to take immediately the necessary steps in order to prevent that crown corporation from broadcasting such evil publicity in favour of crime which is paid for by the state. Some may say that the C.B.C. is an independent corporation beyond government control. I agree. However, this crown corporation is subsidized by public funds which the government has the heavy responsibility of controlling in the best interests of the taxpayers. The latter, far from blaming the government, would be pleased to realize that their government was taking vigorous measures to cancel those shows which had a corrupting influence on their homes and which greatly compromised their children's future.
Before I conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the government that the Gaspe peninsula, and more specifically Bonaventure county which I have the honour to represent for a second term, with a fivefold increase in the number of votes, still have numerous needs. The labourer, the farmer, the fisherman and all the working class are anxiously waiting for tangible improvement of their condition. Nevertheless, the people of my riding are happy that the present government has taken new measures to assist underdeveloped areas. These fiscal incentives and other benefits have largely contributed to the establishment, this spring, of a wood processing plant by the Bathurst Power and Paper Company at a cost of nearly $50 million in my riding, at New Richmond.
As for agriculture, I am glad to see that important legislation is announced in the speech from the throne, including provision for the establishment of a department of rural development which will be entrusted mostly with the agricultural problems of eastern Canada.
Fisheries which are a mainstay of our local economy deserve more consideration on the part of our governments. Thus, Gascons, a
The Address-Mr. Bechard village in the riding of Bonaventure whose sole source of income is fishing, urgently needs a harbour to ensure not only its normal and constant economic development but its very survival. Wharf extensions and repairs are needed throughout the area. Walls should be built to protect both public and private properties against the threat of landslides; in view of the heavy expenses involved the local communities could not afford to finance such works even in part.
Our project which is especially dear to me is the setting up of an air line in the Gaspe area which is deprived of such a service right now. Such a service will be absolutely necessary, considering the present industrial development and the expansion which will be forthcoming. Now that the project for the construction of a railroad between Matane and Ste. Anne des Monts has been shelved, I feel that the central government would work in the best interest of transportation in our district if it established an air line in the Gaspe area. Certain existing private strips could easily be transferred to the public domain and improved later on to provide a service worthy of our district which asks nothing more than to co-operate and to make a greater contribution to the national economy.
To conclude, I would like to offer my colleague from Gaspe and the people throughout the Gaspe peninsula, especially the Canadian Legion, district No. 1 of Gaspe, who is the actual promoter of the plan, my wholehearted support for the building in Gaspe, within the framework of the centennial celebrations, of a replica of the Grande Hermine, on which Jacques Cartier crossed the ocean to land at Gaspe and reach the new world. As all hon. members know, the first pages of Canadian history were written in Gaspe and, for that reason, I am of the opinion that our government should take advantage of the centennial of confederation to proclaim Gaspe as an historical site and participate in the building in Gaspe itself of this historical vessel which, moreover, would be a monument to the glory of one of the founding groups of our country, and a tremendous tourist attraction.
So, with the co-operation of the Canadian government and the permission of Providence, we would be able, in 1967, at the time of the world fair, to visit this ship which would have sailed on the St. Lawrence up to Montreal, proudly hoisting our distinctive national flag.
