subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my remarks, I wish to congratulate the mover (Mr. Cote, Longueuil) and the seconder (Mr. Basford) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Speaking with great sincerity, they dealt with several matters which are of great interest to the Canadian people.
I also wish to take this opportunity to congratulate the new ministers as well as the new parliamentary secretaries, and to extend to them my best wishes for success in their new functions.
Mr. Speaker, in the course of my short speech, I intend to deal with three subjects.
First, I want to talk about parliament and our parliamentary life here in Ottawa; second, about the economy of our country, Canada, and third, about national unity and various matters which interest both the federal government and the provinces of our great and young country, Canada.

Today, Mr. Speaker, in my speech I wish to touch briefly upon three main subjects. First of all I should like to draw attention to certain facts which I believe are relevant to our parliament and to parliamentary life here in Canada today. Second, I wish to outline in a general way some basic considerations involving the economy of our country. Third, I should like to discuss national unity, especially in the context of federal-provincial relations.
Under the heading "parliamentary life", I believe that many of us in this house feel collectively that we often lose touch with the people and their legitimate aspirations. This was what happened in Westminster before the second world war. I do not pretend to lecture or pontificate at the expense of my colleagues in this house, but I do not think I exaggerate when I say that the current parliament often fails to reflect the true feelings of the people and the aspirations of Canadian citizens.
I am not attempting to allocate blame either to the people or to ourselves; I am

simply attempting to enunciate an objective fact. Many speakers, in fine speeches, have suggested changes in the rules, but let us never forget that we in this House of Commons are masters of our own rules, and no rule changes will improve the situation unless good will and common sense prevail at all times.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to touch upon what I consider to be an even more basic and fundamental consideration in relation to the problem at hand. I think many hon. members of this House of Commons have often heard people say, "Oh, we are not really interested in politics. We cannot really see any difference between the parties in the House of Commons". We as members of the House of Commons might know that there is a difference as between the political parties, but let us admit that there is often confusion in the public mind. To a large extent, in my opinion, in the last four elections and in this house we have spent a disproportionate amount of time criticizing one another and conducting negative campaigns, while forgetting to a great extent to really tell the people of Canada what we stand for.
It is my impression, sir, that all parties have the obligation to recreate and remould their thinking in a positive vein. Let us make sure that in the next campaign we present the people with true and positive alternatives. After that it will be the obligation of the press and of the people of Canada to take an even greater interest in our political institutions and to cast off the cloak of cynicism. I fully realize, being ofttimes an unabashed partisan myself, that this will involve for me personally a high degree of self discipline and self denial.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am prepared to admit that. But I would say to hon. members opposite, "Do not clap too hard. I would suggest to you that there is only about five inches between a halo and a noose". I fully realize that contemporary conditions have largely made obsolete some of the classical cleavages which in the past have separated political parties. Also, either in this House of Commons or outside this House of Commons we should not attempt to display differences for differences' sake. But apart from discussing issues, if every party in this house thoroughly examines its doctrines or its principles, as the case may be, and adopts what I conceive to be the true glories of positivism, Canada and the people of Canada will be well served. Whether this is done at a Kingston thinkers' conference or a Port Hope thinkers' conference is immaterial, as far as I am concerned; the obligation is still there.

During and after the last election a great deal of cynicism invaded the body politic of this nation. The Liberal party before, during and after the election, said that serious times were to be dealt with by serious people; serious people must discuss serious questions. Then they presented us with the slick slogan of 60 days of easy decision. Every member in this House of Commons must realize the power of communication media today. We must realize that it is a powerful instrument, and that we can create unnecessarily far too great a degree of expectancy, if you will, in the public mind. We must each of us realize that political programs cannot be sold to the public like soap flakes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I hear some "Oh, oh's" from across the chamber. They undoubtedly denote a guilty conscience, Mr. Speaker. Because differences are not easily perceivable, it does not mean that differences are not there. Again, I repeat, I do hope it is not taken to mean that I have been so presumptuous as to lecture my colleagues in this House of Commons, but I hope that at least some of my remarks this afternoon might prove to be helpful.
I would now like to deal with the second phase of my speech, Mr. Speaker, namely a few general remarks relating to the Canadian economy. Herein I shall underline two positive and basic examples of modern, dynamic Conservative thinking relating to the principle of a property owning democracy and the principle of the government's real role in encouraging individual and national excellence. Before doing so I wish to make reference to some specific points which are of interest to me and, I hope, to other hon. members.
Sir, the basic strength of the Canadian economy is readily apparent when we consider that it survived undoubtedly the worst budget ever presented to the Canadian people. I think I am not exaggerating. Many hon. members and people outside this house have already termed the last budget a national disaster. We can only hope that before the Minister of Finance is permitted to present the Canadian people with another budget he will rely less on reckless experiments and more on experience, for experience is a quality which we Conservatives on this side of the house still feel has much merit. The basic long term objectives of the budget of the Minister of Finance were never fully debated in terms as to whether or not they were sound, because the short term measures that he took to gain, so to speak, these long term objectives were absolutely foolhardy. We on this side of the house will continue to press for the abolish-20220-15
The Address-Mr. Grafftey ment of the tax on certain construction materials and certain machinery entering into production. We will also press for a clarification of what seems to most of us an absolutely ridiculous and untenable stand taken by the government in relation to the withholding tax.
The next general remarks I have to make, Mr. Speaker, I am sure touch the experience of each and every member of this House of Commons. We as members of parliament know, no matter what the indicators say, that there are far too many people in this land who are not truly sharing in Canada's prosperity. Of course we realize that excellence must have its just rewards and that we must continue helping less privileged people and less privileged lands abroad. But in so many ways we have done a poor job right here at home in pushing back the frontiers of want and poverty. We on this side of the house rejoice with the government that the unemployment figures are down. At the same time there is the example of the province of Quebec, where regional unemployment is still a great problem. It is absolutely foolhardy, it is absolutely absurd to quote statistics to people who are out of work, who seek jobs and who are living in want and poverty. Some armchair sophisticates suggest from their ivory towers of affluence that there is a large body of men who do not want to work. It may well be that there are a few exceptions and a few men who do not want to work, but this generalization is just pure nonsense.
Wherever there is economic opportunity all men will willingly work; I repeat; with a a few notable exceptions. In many parts of Canada a number of our people living in great poverty and want do not fall under the aegis of government or private welfare help. This is largely true in so many of our rural areas. These are the masses of the silent, voiceless poor who have never known economic opportunity; and let no cynic say they do not want to work.
On the other hand, let us all join hands in this House of Commons in a bipartisan way and meet this challenge. This challenge must be met; because apart from other implications, if we fail to push back the frontiers of want and unbelievable poverty at home, what is our answer to communism? The challenge is at hand. We are a prosperous country. The answer will not always be easy. There will be no place for sloganeering or demagoguery; but the time to start is now. What does a prosperous Canada mean to the hundreds and thousands of our people living in substandard conditions of want and poverty?
The next question I wish to discuss under the economic heading relates to immigration.
I firmly believe-and this is a personal belief -that for the economic good of our country

The Address-Mr. Gfafftey we need more people. Are we to depend, I ask myself, only upon an increased birth rate to achieve a greater population; or is the government going to adopt a positive immigration policy? On the other hand, does the government feel that such a positive immigration policy would hurt employment prospects? I ask the government why Australia's immigration figures outstripped ours in 1963. Is the government going to adopt an assisted passage program? I ask the government what is the target for immigrants to Canada set by the department for this year. In other words, what is their immigration policy?
The move to have a separate minister in charge of the treasury board is of great interest, Mr. Speaker. It is only fitting that in this day and age detailed consideration should be given to government priorities. I believe that nations are like individuals and have certain capacities and aptitudes. We should give priority to those things which Canada is best suited to do, and this challenge faces the new minister. Only a few reactionaries are left in the country, who think ipso facto that any economic activity on the part of the government is essentially bad. Hospitals, schools, roads, public buildings, bridges and a great many public facilities need immediate completion, and governments are going to carry out these things. The new minister must get on with his job and show us that he is conscientiously planning his priorities, for when there is a great lag between the public and the private sectors of the economy the whole economic health of our nation suffers.
In closing this part of my speech I should like to refer to two principles in which my party deeply believes. While many of us recognize the welfare needs as already cited, we also recognize another great need of the day, namely the necessity for government to play its part in encouraging individual and national excellence. We must balance this notion with the true and rightful demands of the welfare state. We politicians talk loosely of the man in the street, the average man, while sometimes forgetting that every individual, in the economic and in every sense, has a motivation upward. Our schools have realized the necessity for paying attention to the often forgotten brilliant student while keeping educational opportunity open for the many.
The challenge for the government is this. It must play its rightful role in recognizing and encouraging individual and national excellence. Research is only one aspect involved. A government that neglects this challenge simply kills the goose that lays the golden egg. These remarks, sir, are based on a conservative respect for individual dignity and a conservative belief that we should expect
[Mr. Grafftey.l
nothing but the best from our country, from our people and from our government. Individual and national excellence involves no 60 days of easy decision, Mr. Speaker. This has often been said before, and I think it is applicable now. The spark from heaven, who picks it up? The crowd, never; the individual, always.
The last principle under economic considerations involves my party's belief that all individuals should be encouraged to have a property stake in their communities. I do not refer to property in the old fashioned landed sense. The government I supported, for example, encouraged, increased and improved farm, housing and small business loans. Government in co-operation with private enterprise must encourage the advance of a property owning democracy. It is my belief that the Liberals' throne speech leaves little room for the operation of this compelling principle. Property ownership must be encouraged in rural and urban areas.
Property should broadly include, Mr. Speaker, the desirability for Canadians to invest in Canadian enterprise; and government, in co-operation with our stock exchanges and stock commissions, must make it attractive for people, not only in the higher income brackets but for men and women in the lower income brackets, to invest in Canadian enterprises. Small business loans must be further stimulated, and one has but to see our bursting urban and suburban centres to recognize the necessity for encouraging home ownership in our cities as well as in our rural areas. The government must make sure there is no slowing down in the impetus given to farm credit by the former minister of agriculture. All these ideas are formed on our party's belief in a property owning democracy and in the importance of private property rights. Overcentralization by the Liberal party and an apparent lack of awareness of the importance of this principle in the throne speech itself gives many of us real reason to worry.
Finally I wish to touch on some questions relating to national unity, especially within the context of federal-provincial relations. It is self evident that constitutionally both levels of government have specific powers and responsibilities which must be carried out. It was no accident of history that in 1867 Conservative principle created the fact of confederation. Decentralization of powers, the necessity for strong and effective local and provincial governments, the idea of local self-agency-these notions have always underlined Conservative thought.
Between 1957 and 1963 our attitude toward the provinces and municipalities, ARDA, coupled with our initiative in the resources

field, are but examples. This attitude was and will always be based on our belief that very often people at the local level know what is best for themselves and how best to direct their own affairs, while at the same time the federal government must remain strong and constitutionally capable of carrying out its own activities.
Today, Mr. Speaker, one of the great challenges to this government remains in the solution to the problems found in the federal-provincial field. For the government to fail to meet this challenge and to solve many of these problems will only mean that national unity will be hurt. Many of the solutions to our economic problems will go by default; and unfortunately if this is the case the job of nation building will also be unnecessarily delayed. Today we realize that the strength of Canada lies in diversity. Let us say that in many parts of the west the melting pot theory has been operative and a strong and proud Canadianism has developed.
Yet it would be wrong to apply this notion of assimilation and this melting pot theory to the French fact in Canada, either in Quebec or in the rest of the country. We in the province of Quebec harbour an equally strong and proud sense of Canadianism, and Conservative action is always based on the realization of the strength and diversity of our confederation. Unlike a Liberal spokesman who spoke in this house the other day, we do not use the unfortunate word "coexistence", but in this house Conservatives understand the positive attributes of unity in diversity. To a degree the Prime Minister has recognized the problem by making himself directly responsible in this house for federal-provincial problems. Much of what he said in his speech last week was laudable, but speeches and action are two different things.
I fail to realize why anybody should be surprised at the unsatisfactory state of affairs existing between Ottawa and the provinces, especially under the present government. The centralist doctrine of Liberalism, largely put into effect by ex-senior bureaucrats sitting on the treasury benches, leaves no room for a satisfactory solution to the problems of confederation. In the two throne speeches the Liberals have talked about cooperative federalism. They only talked about it, and to a large extent the great failure of their economic programs has been based on their failure to consult with the provinces.
The government consults only under pressure, often unwillingly, and too often after the damage is done. Just last week we saw much unnecessary friction between the Prime 20220-15J
The Address-Mr. Grafftey Minister and the premier of Quebec in relation to the proposed legislation for student loan funds. Where was the proper consultation there? Time and time again during the last session I asked ministers if the provinces were consulted with regard to many pieces of legislation, but there was little or no consultation. Time and time again I put motions on the order paper for the production of papers relating to preparations for federal-provincial conferences touching upon proposed governmental action, and I was absolutely astounded at the lack of preparation.
Mr. Speaker, I am not becoming involved in the old debate as to whether we should be for or against centralization or provincial rights. I am merely underlining the real necessity for consultation. The Prime Minister's initiative in setting up offices under his direction is not enough in this regard. The ARDA approach and the secretariat experience in the resources field must be broadened and extended in the sphere of federal-provincial relations. The Prime Minister knows that one does not go to international meetings without consultation and preparation. If you do not prepare and consult, then the result is failure and disillusionment.
We in Quebec realize it is bad for Canada and Quebec when simultaneously there are Liberal governments in office in Ottawa and in the province of Quebec, because Liberalism has never said the same thing in Quebec as it has here in Ottawa. An hon. member on the Liberal side made a fine speech a few minutes ago but, Mr. Speaker, between the end of last session and the start of this session what did the hon. member for Lotbiniere say, and what did the hon. member for York-Humber say? Let us put an end to this hypocrisy. That is why Mr. Levesque is crying for separation of the Ottawa and Quebec wings of the party.
In the war years when the Liberals were in power here and in Quebec, the Liberal party practically sabotaged national unity with its performance in relation to the conscription crisis. Today the Grits are at it again. As soon as we have had simultaneously Liberal governments in Ottawa and Quebec, national unity has suffered and irresponsible utterances have been divisive. Sir, they must put a stop to it. This is the second time in my short lifetime that we have experienced Liberal governments simultaneously in office in Ottawa and Quebec. This is the second time in a short generation that national unity has been unnecessarily strained by their divisive utterances.
I know some of the Liberal members from Ontario find this hard to understand, but I ask them to come into the province of Quebec

The Address-Mr. Lessard and see how their party performs there. If they do, I doubt if they will sit much longer in the Liberal caucus. This reckless irresponsibility must stop. It is all very well in front of the press gallery for the Prime Minister to make his lovely speeches, and for other hon. members opposite to make their own speeches, but it is a very different cry if one follows them out on to the hustings in Quebec and sees the great difference in what they say there.
We on the Conservative side realize that the basic fabric of our confederation is too strong to succumb. Here on this side of the house, realizing the nature of confederation, we are working along the road to our party s return to power in Ottawa. The government must not only talk about co-operative federalism but it must act, and act now. Even centralists, however unwillingly, must understand the compelling necessity to consult, and also the nature of the problem.
In this debate on the throne speech we attempt to reflect the thinking of our people, their aspirations, and the mood of the time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin my remarks on the contents of the speech from the throne by congratulating the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the message read by His Excellency the Governor General at the opening of this session. I congratulate them, first of all, for the trust put in their ability by their leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) who awarded them this task, and also for their way of carrying it out.
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey), who preceded me, I applauded the attitude just taken to the effect that we should banish party politics from the house and future elections.
However, I am sorry that in the last part of his remarks he should have let the worse side of his personality take over and air the virulent partisan views to which we had become accustomed from him, a practice which he himself admitted.
Mr. Speaker, the legislative program submitted by the government did not reveal any new plan for efficiently fighting unemployment. Practically all the proposed legislation was already contained in last year's speech from the throne. Moreover, some projects formulated but not discussed at that time seem to have been either forgotten or shelved this year.

Every Canadian will still remember the election promises which the authorized spokesmen of the Liberal party made, and more particularly the elimination of unemployment.
The corner stone of Liberal policy to revive our economy consisted in the creation of a municipal loan bank and the setting up of an economic development corporation.
The municipal loan board was instituted last year, but it lacks the suggested scope, and its operations up to now have not been anything to speak of and did not have the expected results.
The economic development corporation was not even set up. Its creation has been withdrawn from the list of sessional business. It seems that, in this respect, the corner stone of the Liberal program proved to be a block of ice which quickly melted away during the summer under the warm rays of the sun, or perhaps in the heated discussion or red-hot pressure of certain groups and interests to which the Minister of Finance had to submit after his budget speech.
This corporation was to create new industries and save those which were shaky; it was going to be also the very instrument that the government intended to use to prevent foreign control over our economy.
Recently, the Financial Post published a striking list of the various Canadian companies which have fallen into foreign hands these last two years, a list to which new names can be added every day.
Just recently, as everybody knows, a Canadian bank fell under American control. Even today, we are on the point of losing one of our large breweries; fortunately, there will be some others left to us, otherwise the Canadian population would certainly suffer from thirst.
But what are we doing, Mr. Speaker, to stop this economic haemorrhage?
Where are the patriotic spirit and the pride of our Canadians?
We hear people talk about economic independence, not to say simply independence. They talk about the serious chronic unemployment which plagues us, about the need to create new primary and secondary industries, about the urgent need to balance our external trade accounts. We claim to have a voice in the various international meetings and organizations.
But, Mr. Speaker, what sense is there in ah those claims? When shall we understand that in economics, just as in medicine, it is necessary to get to the cause of the disorder in order to cure the patient, to get him strong again.

The 19 million Canadians to whom we, in this house, are responsible for the conduct of the affairs of the country, expect us to put aside partisanship and to settle down to the task with that broadness of mind that every man should have who has been given the responsibility of representing his fellow citizens in the administration of his country.
I, for one, intend to take my responsibilities and even to make suggestions likely to be considered on their merits in the search for solutions to our problems.
I should like first of all to reiterate my confidence in the efficiency of private enterprise. But this confidence does not prevent me from seeing the deficiencies and recommending action on the part of public bodies and governments, when private enterprise will not tackle the job.
On the other hand, all private enterprise promoters say that if they lack initiative in setting up new enterprises or in enlarging those they already own and operate, it is because of the ever-growing burden of taxes of all kinds that reduces reinvestment opportunities. Moreover, all Canadians complain, as they well might, about this constant increase of taxes.
In view of those facts, what should we do? Knowing that the Minister of Finance is preparing his budget and that he must surely be looking for suggestions, I should like to humbly offer this one.
In order to encourage all Canadians to work harder for our economic recovery, a system should be developed which would provide for a tax reduction on corporation profits equal to 25 per cent of the increase in that tax revenue due to the annual increase in our national production.
Another 25 per cent would go to the taxpayers and the remaining 50 per cent would remain in the treasury to meet the normal increase in the administrative expenditures of the country.
It would be a kind of rebate or dividend, a reward directly and proportionately related to the collective effort and action of the people to raise the growth rate of our economy.
On Monday, the Minister of Labour gave us a somewhat optimistic view of the present situation and of the good effects produced by the different pieces of legislation he introduced and applied since he took office in order to reduce seasonal unemployment. To mention only one of those measures, the $500 bonus granted to the owners of houses built during the winter months seems to have been a sound step to keep construction workers on the job. But in Saguenay, as in many other regions across the country, that measure will
The Address-Mr. Lessard not be profitable because the need of new houses is not felt in designated areas since the people have already started to move out; and for every project carried out this winter there will be a proportional increase of unemployment next summer.
Mr. Speaker, since the minister succeeded to maintain winter employment and even to increase it, could he tell us what concrete action he is contemplating to fight summer unemployment, since it seems that in endeavouring to correct a situation, we are in the process of aggravating another one? If we carry out during the winter months part of the projects which normally gave jobs to our workers during the summer, we are only spreading more evenly the total amount of work to be carried out in that field of the building industry.
To date, I regret that most of the measures introduced and applied have only shifted the problems.
Mr. Speaker, at the risk of repeating what has already been said I say that only the development of secondary industries in these manufacturing sectors where we are importing our consumer goods can offer a permanent solution.
Everyone here, I believe, recognizes this fact. Then, what are we waiting for before taking necessary action? Measures are required to prevent foreign control, since the matter is very serious, for there is no point in building up our economy if, afterwards, it falls into the hands of foreigners.
Taxation reduction? Yes. And what for? Because it is the consumer who regulates production and we should increase his buying power.
Easy credit to encourage investments? Yes, through the economic development bank, in order that small enterprise, industries in general, may prosper and expand.
Technical aid? Yes. The government can ensure this aid thanks to all the talents it has at its disposal; it can reduce the companies' costs by supplying them with technical information at a comparatively lower price.
Research on foreign markets? It is especially in that field the federal government should assert itself, so that markets be developed in order that our industry may find the outlets necessary to support its production.
Export credit for economically weak nations? On that point, it is evident, and quite interesting to note, that Canada will be unable to compete successfully in countries where the economy has been highly developed. We should then look towards the less-favoured countries and really conquer markets if we want to help our country expand.

The Address-Mr. Lessard
These are the concrete measures liable to bring the results we all wish.
Not only the government but all the intermediate bodies of society should participate in the struggle.
I would particularly like to stress the important new role that the labouring classes and their organizations, that is the unions, should play. I would like our labour leaders to look beyond collective demands when they sit at the bargaining table and to indulge in a new field of action, which would serve to prove and to test some theories which the labour movement has used as a basis since its inception, that is profit sharing.
In an economic system, certain factors are elementary but essential to its proper function. The workers have and could reasonably control two of those important factors. They are both producers and consumers, but they do not have the financial control at present. Consequently, at this stage in the evolution of social-economic thinking, it would be advisable for our union leaders to take up a new role. They should contribute to the development of those secondary industries we so badly need and which, precisely, depend on the understanding and co-operation of unions in order to compete successfully and develop. Since the development of industry is a guarantee of the survival and prosperity of unions, the latter have every reason to contribute to that development.
All union workers could contribute, through their central unions, to an industrial fund invested in industry by means of secured bonds, of privileged and common shares, which would give them a strong voice in business planning and administration.
We have reached a point, I believe, where union leaders and workers must realize that the time for demands is over to some extent and that they now must extend the field of their activities. Workers in general must consider that they not only have rights and prerogatives, but that they also have duties and responsibilities.
Some will rightly say, I know, that heads of businesses also have duties and responsibilities that they failed to carry out and try to evade; but because some people do not assume or understand their responsibilities towards their country and their fellow citizens, this is no excuse for other groups or for the workers.
By doing so, the workers would partially solve a problem which affects them first of all. They would thus positively prove their desire to co-operate with the authorities of the country and the industry to build a strong Canada of which they would actually be the rightful co-owners.
[Mr. Lessard (Lake St. John) .1
Therefore, it is incumbent on all Canadians to relinquish certain antiquated ideas and act in such a way that common interest will prevail over sectarian, regional or even racial interests.
Other problems have evidently also retained my attention. But there will be many other opportunities during this session to express my views and those of my fellow citizens.
I would have liked to point out the advantages and the problems of my riding of Lake St. John but my fellow citizens will forgive my not mentioning them at this time, because I consider that our problems in Saguenay are closely related to the problems of Canada as a whole and that I must depart from this narrow-mindedness, this parochial spirit, and consider things from a national standpoint. In the past, members from Quebec have too often, unfortunately, showed interest solely in matters pertaining to the street where they were born.
If we, Quebeckers, sincerely want our opinions to be listened to and agreed to, we must try to consider the problems from the national point of view instead of a local one.
In eastern Canada, agriculture is in a rather precarious situation and I hope that the government will very soon introduce the bill concerning the establishment of the rural development department. Then, we will have the opportunity to express our views and to make suggestions.
The constitutional problems and all the discussions we are witnessing at this time are disturbing me also. But, in view of the complexity of this subject, I shall be very cautious in discussing it.
I think that too many terse statements have already been made by irresponsible people who are completely unaware of all the facts and who unfortunately get favourable press reports at home and elsewhere. For this reason, I shall refrain from making any statement, as I am only a layman in the matter, save for this brief comment.
We speak of a pact, an agreement, a treaty or a constitution which should be rethought or reviewed. Sometimes I wonder why? I believe that whatever agreement is arrived at, its implementation and success will depend entirely upon the honesty and the principles of the men who will carry it out.
It is men who must be reformed first of all and above everything else. Let us go back to the Christian principles that we should never have forgotten. It is useless to think of changing legislation, rules, agreements, if we do not accept to change ourselves and to come back to the principles of love for our neighbour and love of justice.

Hatred and discrimination brought about recently the tragic death of a statesman whom we all admired, Mr. John F. Kennedy. What are we waiting for to regain our senses? That our conscience be burdened with the death of innocent victims?
Mr. Speaker, I leave it up to the hon. members and to all Canadians who will read my thoughts to draw their own conclusions.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to discuss other problems in which I am interested but I know the time of the house is valuable. Besides, most of those problems have been or will be dealt with by my colleagues.
I close my remarks with a word of thanks to the house for its kind attention.

I should like first, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate my colleagues the mover and seconder of the address in reply upon the excellence of their speeches.
I was pleased to note that the speech from the throne contained a reference to amendments to improve the National Housing Act. I would have been even happier if those proposed amendments had been brought before this house during the last session as had been hoped, but unfortunately that did not prove possible.
The National Housing Act contains among its other provisions the legislation governing urban renewal and redevelopment in Canada, and it is in this field that I have a particular interest. First as an alderman in the city of Hamilton, and now as a member of this house, I have been privileged to represent a group of citizens, more than 8,000 in all, who are being directly affected by urban renewal. In addition, for the past three years I have been a member of the Hamilton urban renewal committee. This experience, sir, has given me what is almost a unique opportunity to acquaint myself with the strengths and weaknesses of our present legislation, from the viewpoint of both a municipal representative and a member of parliament.
From this close acquaintance I have arrived at a number of criticisms of the National Housing Act as it is now constituted, but these are, I hope, constructive criticisms; because I also have some proposals for amending the act in ways which would greatly benefit Canadian municipalities, while at the same time strengthening our national economy, providing expanded employment opportunities and helping to meet the housing needs of medium to low income families as well as many newly arrived Canadians from European countries.
These may appear to be rather broad claims to make for any revised legislation, but they can be backed up by facts, figures
The Address-Mr. Macaluso and actual experiences to what I am sure will be the satisfaction of every member of this house.
Let us first look at Hamilton's present urban renewal project, the city's second, in the north end. It is one of the largest ever to be undertaken in Canada, covering some 260 acres of primarily residential land in one of the oldest areas of the city. More to the point, this project is the first of its kind in this country, accenting as it does the preservation-and I emphasize the word "preservation"-of an area through rehabilitation and improvements rather than the bulldozing which has been practised until now. We happen to believe that this new approach to urban renewal is one which will have much wider application in cities and towns across Canada than the former total clearance technique. But, just because of this pioneering, the city and the residents of the area are being penalized by the legislation as it is now written. While paying lip service to the ideal of improving and maintaining our urban areas rather than demolishing them, the Act and the agency charged with administering it, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, are actually forcing cities into levelling homes and displacing families with great financial and social losses.
The north end project in Hamilton is going to cost more than $8 million. On the surface one might suppose that, the way the National Housing Act is written, the federal treasury would pick up $4 million of that bill and that the remainder would be split evenly between the city and the province, since that is what the Ontario legislation provides. If you were to reach such a conclusion, however, you would be very much mistaken, Mr. Speaker. Instead, Ottawa is paying only about $2 million, the province about $1 million, and the city is forced to carry the remainder of $5 million.
In other words, because Hamilton is making an honest, well planned and highly lauded effort to preserve valuable housing stock and prevent the break-up of families, it is being penalized to the tune of $3 million. Further, you can be sure that no other municipality is going to commit itself to a program of improvement as opposed to a program of destruction while the present situation exists.
How has this come about? Well, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the present Minister of National Revenue are empowered to participate to the extent of half the cost of buying and demolishing buildings in a declared redevelopment area, but they cannot contribute one cent to the improvement of such an area by providing the services and amenities required and helping area residents

The Address-Mr. Macaluso help themselves. All of this is left to the overburdened municipal taxpayer.
Therefore the first amendment I would suggest for the National Housing Act would be one to permit full participation-and I emphasize the word "full"-by federal authorities in well balanced urban renewal programs which provide not only for clearance but also for the general upgrading of a neighbourhood. This would mean financial participation in the provision of essential services-roads, schools, parks, sewers and so on-required to bring about lasting improvements.
Following directly from this point is the second amendment required to make urban renewal an effective tool for the over-all betterment of the older sections of our cities. It would provide aid, advice and active financial support to home owners in these declining areas who wish to maintain and improve their properties. For these people more liberal home improvement loans would be helpful, and National Housing Act mortgage loans on old houses would be an absolute boon.
The extension of National Housing Act loans to older properties would probably do as much as any other conceivable piece of legislation to halt the spread of decay and the growth of slums in our urban areas. It would make it possible for people to afford houses in the central areas of our cities instead of forcing them out to the suburbs. It would save thousands of Canadians from falling into the hands of unscrupulous speculators and mortgage firms who exact exorbitant interest rates plus bonuses and penalties from purchasers whose only wish is to live up to the great Canadian ideal of home ownership. Properly drafted, such an amendment would permit many of our low income families to own their own homes for the first time, because the National Housing Act mortgage would permit a low down payment they could meet, and would, I hope, make provision for the necessary house improvements to be covered by the mortgage payments.
Let me add that there is another hidden bonus in such a step. The making available of money to update or rehabilitate older houses could create many thousands of year round jobs in the building trades and allied industries. To go back for a moment to Hamilton's north end project, it has been estimated that private home improvements generated in that area of the city's urban renewal program will probably amount to more than $2 million. That sum, remember, is the amount expected to be spent in private home improvements in one area of one city because of a well balanced renewal program. I leave it to the members of this house to apply such projections to their own municipalities and to contemplate what that could

mean in terms of goods and services and particularly jobs across Canada.
Now I would like to suggest a third amendment to the National Housing Act which could, by itself, do as much to spur on the national economy as any other action which could be undertaken by this house. I am speaking of the extension of federal urban renewal legislation to cover commercial redevelopment, specifically the redevelopment of our downtown areas.
In support of this recommendation I would point out that two out of every three Canadians now live in an urban area, a city or town. Before 1980 it is fully expected that this will rise to three out of every four. This means that the problems which face our municipalities are of very real concern to every one of us here. We all know these problems; rapid growth in the suburbs coupled with decay in the core; traffic congestion; unprecedented demands for municipal services; and above all, skyrocketing municipal tax rates. These are not new problems, nor are they ones which are going to solve themselves. They will not go away if we ignore them.
There is probably no other body in the nation which has dug deeper into these municipal problems and spent more time and expert knowledge on finding solutions to them than the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. In recent years delegations from the federation have told this present government and earlier ones that the extension of urban renewal programs to the commercial core areas of our cities could be of inestimable benefit to our cities, that every dollar of public money spent in such programs would generate several dollars of private investment. Our Canadian mayors are not taking a wild stab in the dark when they make such a recommendation. They have seen what renewal activities in old, deteriorating downtown areas can mean in terms of new sources of municipal tax revenue, and consequent decreased tax demands on individual home owners. They know the record in the United States, where taxes from redeveloped downtown areas have jumped from six to ten times over previous levels, and city after city has the same success story to tell.
I sincerely trust, Mr. Speaker, that the amendments to the National Housing Act proposed by this government and promised in this house do take an enlightened approach to the problems of our urban citizens and taxpayers; that they do incorporate at least the few improvements which I have suggested here today: first, federal financial participation in improving a neighbourhood and providing services and amenities over and above

The Address-Mr. Crouse
total clearance; second, the extension of National Housing Act mortgage loans to cover older homes in redevelopment areas as a first step to extending this program to National Housing Act mortgages throughout cities for older homes; third, urban renewal aid to municipalities wishing to undertake downtown commercial redevelopment.
I trust, too, that these amendments will be introduced into this house at the earliest possible date so that, in company with the provinces and municipalities of Canada, we can clear blight, provide decent housing, boost the economy and cut unemployment, all things which improved urban renewal legislation can help us to achieve. This legislation which is proposed in the Speech from the Throne is of a type that certainly all of us in this house realize is of invaluable benefit to all citizens across this country. It is a piece of legislation which certainly should not be treated controversially or in a partisan manner on the part of any hon. member of this house.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I urge the party leaders on both sides of the house to get together and arrange for the introduction of this legislation as soon as possible. The City of Hamilton has been waiting for one year for federal legislation such as this to proceed with their renewal program. I am sure there are many communities and cities across this country that are waiting for this legislation. I can name Halifax and Sault Ste. Marie. London, Ontario, is undergoing urban renewal and-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to congratulate the hon. member for Longueuil and the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard for the capable manner in which they discharged their duties in moving and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They were indeed given a difficult task. In Nova Scotia, when a fisherman hauls in his net and finds nothing in it, he calls it a water haul. This throne speech represented a water haul in so far as this administration is concerned, for it contained little to excite the daring, to test the strong, or give new promise to the timid, as stated by the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) when he was made Prime Minister.
I will say this for the Grits, that they struck out boldly with the Prime Minister's high line of 60 days of decision, but the line must have snapped. They are now floundering desperately in water beyond their depth. They have found that election gimmicks are no substitute for policy, and their performances fall far short of their promises. The only thing sustaining the present Liberal government is the sound policies established by the former Conservative administration when in office.
The Prime Minister in his speech took comfort from the fact that unemployment in some regions was lower than when he took office, and that our trade with all countries last year exceeded $13,500 million, the highest ever recorded. I am sure he will be the first to agree that much of this trade expansion is due to the efforts of the previous administration to encourage more exports by Canadian manufacturers, along with the beneficial effects of the devalued dollar. Oh, how they ridiculed this move. Liberal speakers during the last two election campaigns when speaking in my riding said this act would bankrupt Canada. They also said that deficit financing should be discontinued and that Canadians should vote Liberal to get the economy rolling again; but they did not say which way.
That was the hue and cry that was spread across the length and breadth of this nation. And what was the result? We will still have budget deficits; the largest, this year, in Canada's peacetime history. And we have a minority Liberal government sitting on the treasury benches, elected on a chain of promises which they have not fulfilled and will not fulfil.
History can now record that our policies were correct; and the fact that the Liberals in office have adopted, or propose to adopt, many of them proves the soundness of our program. Here I refer to the extension of our program to build vocational schools to retrain our unemployed in new skills. They talk of the establishment of a national pension plan as though it were something new. When we were in office our leader initiated a study to establish a pension plan that would be acceptable to all the provinces. The reform of the Senate and measures to strengthen the position of periodicals published in Canada are two more Conservative proposals. They have continued the policy which we initiated to sell our surplus agricultural products, such as wheat, to communist China and other communist countries.
When the Conservative government started this program, what did the Liberals do? They started a rumour and raised suspicion right

The Address-Mr. Crouse across Canada that we were not going to be paid for this wheat. "It is a giveaway", they charged. But, in office, these stones which the builders rejected in opposition have now become the cornerstone of their policies. They have set their sails and are following, to some degree, the course we plotted when in office.
However, in my opinion Canada today is like a ship caught up in a hurricane. Its destiny depends more upon the skill of the men at the wheel than upon the driving force of its engines. The crew of the good ship Canada are today concerned, and rightly so, because since the April election they have seen that the men at the wheel are weak, confused and indecisive. How else can you explain legislation introduced and then withdrawn; programs announced and then amended; taxes levied and then changed, thereby creating a chaotic tax jungle and the most uncertain, perplexing, frustrating situations ever experienced by Canadian businessmen? There was never a time in Canada's history when decisive leadership was more required; and never in our history was there less leadership material available in government. Parliament, and the Canadian people in the briefs presented to this government, are calling out for a captain, a leader with a knowledge of our problems and a desire to act, not politically but decisively for the benefit of all Canada. Since it is evident that the government is not capable of supplying this leadership, it is therefore up to the official opposition to point out the way that should be followed by the present government.
Let us look at unemployment, for example. The present government prefers to look at existing unemployment, which exceeds over 500,000 people, as a regional rather than a national problem. We still have serious unemployment in Canada. I hold in my hand the dominion bureau of statistics bulletin dated February 21, in which is stated:
Claimants for unemployment insurance benefit numbered 532,300 on December 31, 1963.
This represented 7 per cent of our labour force. Unemployment in the Atlantic area is still an urgent matter; 12.6 per cent of the labour force were jobless last month in the Atlantic area, compared with the national level of 7 per cent.
While the trend has been toward a more vigorous economy, the continuing spectre of intolerably high unemployment still casts a sobering shadow over the regional scene. Two avenues are open to us. We must develop new and stronger measures which will aid the Atlantic provinces' economic growth, or strengthen existing legislation embodied in the Economic Council of Canada, the area

development agency within the new Department of Industry, the federal government's ARDA program and the Atlantic development board. Here I should like to endorse the remarks made last evening by the hon. member for Cumberland, when he referred to the Atlantic development board and stated that it required additional funds. I agree with him, because the present funds which have been made available to the Atlantic development board are certainly insufficient to cope with the problems in this vast area.
In my opinion the problems of our eastern farmers should be of immediate concern to the present government. According to recent statistics, over 10 per cent of our labour force is employed in Canadian agriculture. However, in Nova Scotia our farm population is dropping. We have little more than 4,000 full-time farmers out of a total of approximately 25,000 farm population and an over-all population nearing 800,000. Our agricultural industry is declining in relative importance. It is declining in terms of our over-all provincial income. We know that agriculture is going through revolutionary changes and endless adjustments, but we also know that practically the same degree of evolution has occurred in other primary industries. This is the age of automation, and farmers are not the only ones who have to come to grips with the realities of a changing world.
The future of our Nova Scotia farmers depends on much more specialization, more emphasis on know-how and management ability. It is in these fields that the federal government can provide more assistance, more research; for after all it is our farmers who, in the final analysis, must provide the greater portion of the food which will be required by a vastly expanding population. Ways must be found to make our marginal lands more productive. Tree farms must be encouraged to fill our future demands for timber and pulp. Fish ponds can be established to augment our farmers' incomes through the sale of trout to our expanding urban areas; and the breeding of partridge and pheasant should not be overlooked as a source of income, as there is a growing demand for these game birds in our present society.
In Nova Scotia today there is an undersupplied local market in most of our basic agricultural products. This applies to our dairy products, beef, hogs, some small fruits and greenhouse crops, and no real marketing problem exists in these areas of production. Our dairy herds have fallen off, and are only two thirds of their number 10 years ago; and though we have had hog promotional programs which resulted in 100,000 hogs being marketed in 1963, there is still a market for another

200,000 hogs, which means a potential $9 million industry for Nova Scotia. Similar opportunities exist in the raising of beef cattle.
Questions may well be asked regarding our lack of progress in these fields. The answer, of course, lies in the profit margin. Our local prices are based on national prices plus the cost of transportation. Our only hope for making profits lies in reducing our production costs and increasing the efficiency of our farm operations. It is absolutely essential that our production costs be brought down to the level of our competitors if we are to expand the growth of eastern agriculture and provide a comparable standard of living to our Nova Scotian farmers in relation to the incomes derived from other industries. For years eastern farmers have provided an assured market for some of the grain grown in our prairie provinces. Recent sales to communist countries have lessened this dependency on eastern markets, but we cannot allow these sales to increase the price of our feed grains to Nova Scotia farmers.
The present grain marketing board in the west is without question functioning efficiently on behalf of the western farmers. In my opinion, we need a similar grain marketing agency for eastern farmers, and for Nova Scotia farmers in particular. Our present grain storage facilities at Halifax, for example, of approximately 4,100,000 bushels, covers only about two thirds of our yearly requirements. We use about six million bushels per year, and we need additional grain storage facilities in Nova Scotia so that we can take advantage of low cost water borne freight provided by the St. Lawrence seaway.
This is an absolute necessity if we are to receive any benefits from the seaway. Additional storage facilities in the east would ease the burden on our western farmers at harvest time and provide Nova Scotia farmers with low cost feed grains, which are absolutely essential if we are to maintain and expand our beef and hog production. The agency could also provide a stable price for our farmers who are planning a 12-month feeding program. Once the eastern grain marketing agency was established they could determine the proper location for additional storage facilities throughout the Atlantic area.
In my opinion, one of these storage elevators should be established in the town of Bridgewater in Lunenburg county. Situated on the beautiful La Have river, this fast growing shopping area serves as the hub of the farming area of Lunenburg and North Queens counties. Low cost water borne grain stored at Bridgewater would provide additional stimulus to the agricultural economy of both counties, and I hope the government will give 20220-16J
The Address-Mr. Crouse serious consideration to this suggestion when it introduces the measures referred to in the speech from the throne for the improvement of farm income.
I note with interest that the government plans to introduce a measure that will enable students to secure loans without interest during their years of university study. While I favour this measure, which will no doubt be of assistance to many students who through no fault of their own are otherwise unable to finance their education, I cannot help but wonder which is the more important, aid to students or aid to universities. In recent years we have seen a tremendous growth in all our universities, and there is a need for continued expansion if we are to accommodate all those desirous of a higher education.
Dalhousie University at Halifax, for example, has an enrolment at present of almost 3,000, and it is expected that the student body will double within the next ten years unless steps are taken to curtail registration. In fact if immediate steps are not taken to increase the present facilities and teaching staff, something along this line will have to be done. A similar situation exists at St. Francis Xavier, Acadia and other maritime institutions of learning, and funds must be found to provide the necessary facilities and professors.
At the present time we in Nova Scotia are labouring under a serious disability in connection with the federal university grants program. We have a high student enrolment in relation to our provincial population, and as a result we have received grants well below the national average. In fact Nova Scotia stands at the bottom of the list, receiving $214 per student last year as compared with $360 in Ontario. The Halifax Chronicle-Herald, in an editorial under date of February 13, commented on this situation as follows:
One of the several persuasive arguments for a federal university grants formula based on college enrolments, rather than provincial populations, rests, as far as Nova Scotia is concerned, on the fact that our institutions of higher learning attract many students from outside the province and indeed the country. This inflow of students combined with the eagerness of native Nova Scotians to attend college, contributes to the province's high student-general population ratio and thus to the correspondingly reduced federal grants which every provincial university receives.
This is a problem which successive governments at Ottawa have failed to rectify, and I cannot urge too strongly upon the present government the need for prompt action on this urgent matter.
I also note in the throne speech that the government plans to introduce proposals to reform the railway system. While I hope

The Address-Mr. Crouse these proposals will result in a reduction of freight rates for the Atlantic provinces, I cannot help but wonder why no consideration has been given to improving our air line services.
When the Prime Minister was speaking in Milford, Nova Scotia, during one of the recent election campaigns, he was deeply concerned with the West Indies trade and a policy calculated to make the Atlantic provinces full partners in confederation. In so far as West Indian trade is concerned he said:
The Liberals want to get that going again. This may require special Canadian aid to the West Indies, especially since the current $10 million aid program expires on March 31.
Whatever happened to this promise? There was no mention of it in last year's throne speech, and in this year's throne speech it is curiously absent again. I would like to remind the Prime Minister that we in the Atlantic provinces can well remember the economic benefits that accrued to our area when trade between Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island and the West Indies was flourishing. I would urge him to do everything possible to expand the West Indies trade in keeping with the start made by the previous Conservative administration.
I suggest that a start can be made in keeping this promise by improving the air service between Halifax and the West Indies. At present Nova Scotians must fly from Halifax to Montreal in order to make connections by air to Bermuda and the West Indies. Since the Atlantic provinces are natural partners with the West Indies, air services between the two areas should be viewed as an economic necessity. So far as T.C.A. is concerned, we are still the forgotten mari-times.
To back up that statement I would like to quote from an article which appeared on February 24 in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, which reads:
Once more the Atlantic provinces have missed out in the promotion efforts of Trans-Canada Air Lines in the British press.
A two-page advertising colour spread it has run in The Sunday Times, described in advance as the beginning of the "biggest ever" U.K. campaign to make known the attractions of 'The Big Holiday Country', mentions every part of Canada except the maritimes.. .even though it takes one hour and $42...less to fly from London to Halifax than to Montreal, the city which gets the special mention as the Canadian gateway.
This cannot be tolerated, and I hope the government will give serious consideration to this problem so that closer air links between Nova Scotia and the Caribbean will become the national policy of Canada.
I also note with interest the government's intention to establish a 12 mile limit for the

Canadian fisheries. While all those who are engaged in the fishing industry will welcome this move, I would again point out the necessity of securing agreement to this proposal from the United States, which purchases approximately 70 per cent of Canada's entire fish production. In my opinion it would be a hollow victory for Canadian fishermen if present friendly relations between Canadian and American fishermen became strained over this measure, because we must depend upon the U.S. market to absorb almost three quarters of our yearly catch.
In the past year the landed value of Nova Scotia's fishing industry alone reached a record height of $35 million, and any restrictions placed upon our sales in the United States market, as a result of the unilateral action of this government in establishing a 12 mile limit, could have disastrous effects on our economy and our expanding fishing fleet. I hope the minister is prepared to give the house an assurance of American concurrence in his proposal when he introduces this legislation.
I also note the government plans to undertake a national fisheries development program, following consultation with the provinces. As the minister is aware, the greatest problem facing our east coast fishing industry at present is the large number of foreign trawlers and draggers operating on our fishing grounds. The Russian fishing fleet alone is estimated in excess of 400 ships, and these are operating very close to the coasts of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. This fleet is serviced by several mother ships, which are high powered floating fish factories of up to 3,000 gross tons. Using stern trawls, they are scooping up vast quantities of fish, and charges have been made in Canada and the United States that the Soviets are using nets with a mesh size smaller than allowed by international agreement. Samples of Russian nets have been picked up with a mesh so small even a sardine could not escape.
If our fisheries resources are to be maintained, the whole issue of fisheries conservation must be further discussed at the international level, and some agreement must be reached on international fisheries law enforcement. If an international inspection team is not set up there will be a gradual diminishing of returns of our fishermen due to overfishing, and a further drain on one of Nova Scotia's most valuable natural resources.
I am also concerned over the future of one of our biggest dollar earners, the lobster. Last year some 36 million pounds of lobsters were caught. These were sold in the United States and Canada, and under a new process many were flown to the European markets. They brought in almost $18 million to our Nova

Scotian fishermen. Over the years much has been learned about the habits of the lobster, and research scientists are constantly trying to throw more light on this finless delicacy of the deep. They claim that tests show lobsters do not travel very far in any given area. However, I believe one of the reasons they are plentiful along the south coast of Nova Scotia is due to the proximity of George's and Brown's banks, and the stocks of large lobsters in that area. I believe strong currents carry small lobsters from these banks close to the shores of Nova Scotia, thereby helping to reseed the grounds annually. Lobsters weighing 20 pounds or more have been brought to the surface by scallop draggers operating on George's and Brown's banks, ana some of these were covered with thousands of small eggs. Without some international agreement or conservation measure, these large seed lobsters may well be destroyed, thereby affecting the future of one of the largest sources of income for our inshore fishermen.
Now that the C.G.S. Hudson has been commissioned and Canada has one of the most modern oceanographic ships afloat, I would urge the government to make use of this ship to provide assistance to our fishing industry. This was part of our intention when the Conservative government established the oceanographic base at Halifax. Though our fishermen landed approximately 16 million pounds of scallops from a fleet of 40 ships last year, I would point out that the fleet is still growing as a result of the Conservative government's shipbuilding program, and new scallop beds must be found in order to meet the demand. Markets are also expanding for swordfish, porbeagle shark, whale and tuna, and it is hoped that the new oceanographic base will set up a research program to help explore untapped areas wherein these fish may be found.
When the Conservative government was in office we instituted strong measures for the advancement of the economy in the Atlantic provinces. Two of these measures were the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants and the implementation of a subsidized shipbuilding program. As a result our shipyards are booming with the construction of steel and wooden trawlers, and secondary industry is being established in Nova Scotia.
But, Mr. Speaker, our policies cannot be expected to carry the Liberals through their whole term in office. When are they going to do something to revive Canada's deep sea fleet? It is now down to three ships and is in danger of disappearing entirely unless changes are made in Canada's tax structure providing more incentive for risk capital. Such aid would be most valuable to our ship-
The Address-Mr. Rondeau yards and our mariners. Rather than continue subsidizing foreign ship owners by building icebreakers to keep the St. Lawrence open on a year round basis, lets use the money to build up our own merchant fleet.
When are they going to make a start on the 35 unfulfilled promises, as listed in the last election campaign and placed on the record last Friday by the hon. member for Yukon? Were these pledges meant to be kept or were they just words to win an election? I remind the government that this is no time for complacency. There is much to be done, and it is their responsibility to get on with the job.
There is little in the throne speech that will be beneficial to the Atlantic provinces, that will provide employment or serve as a brake against inflation and the rising cost of living. When he presented his budget last year-and many Canadians hoped it would be his last budget-the Minister of Finance said:
If we are afraid to face reality, if we are afraid to take the actions and the decisions that are called for. then the consequences cannot be long delayed.
At the present rate of progress in implementing their pledges, there can be little doubt what the consequences will be to the present administration when they must again face the electorate.
