speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish, first of all, to congratulate the mover (Mr. Cote, Longueuil) and the seconder (Mr. Basford) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Last Tuesday we heard the speech read by His Excellency at the opening of the second session of the twenty sixth parliament of Canada. That speech, the second since the Liberal party came into power on April 8, namely ten months after the stable team of the Liberal government took office, enables us to realize that the Liberal team in Ottawa is, in fact, stability itself.
If we refer to the Larousse dictionary, the word "stability" is so defined: It can be said that a team is stable if it does not go forward nor backwards, neither to the right nor to the left. If we apply this definition to the Pearson team, this is the finest example of immobility itself.
We have learned at least one thing from the speech from the throne, that is that the government intends to establish a department of rural development.
An analysis of the agricultural problem in Canada shows that it is not limited only to the wheat problem of western Canada, but

The Address-Mr. Rondeau includes also the agricultural problems of eastern Canada.
When considering this agricultural problem, we sometimes wonder why it is intended to establish a department of rural development, since a department of rural displacement would be much more suitable to the agricultural class in 1964.
When newspapers report that each week, in my district, the eastern townships, 25 to 50 farmers have to auction off their land because they are unable to meet their obligations and make a living with their income, I say to myself that the establishment of a rural displacement department would be quite indicative of the Liberals' agriculture policy.
I remember that 15 years ago, after the war, farmers in my district used to go and buy a new tractor or some other piece of farm machinery right after seeding time. They would pay $500 down and undertake to pay the balance in the fall.
In early November, after collecting their income from the crop of tobacco, sugar beets, string beans, peas and tomatoes, and from the dairy industry, they paid the balance owing on the tractor or some other farm implement.
There is no such thing today. You will find that farmers no longer buy or pay with their income, because it is non-existent. You will see, however, that goods are bought through mortgage loans which have swallowed up the farmers for the past ten years.
What solution is offered by the Liberal party that teems with economists who thought they could work wonders as soon as they came into office in Ottawa? What are the solutions advocated by the Liberal economists regarding the farming problem? They merely say to farmers: Produce more. You have butter spoiling in storage and $4 million are paid in taxes each year for the storage of unsold butter.
While the solution of economists is to produce more, that of the Creditistes is more logical and can be summarized as follows: Let us sell more goods by enabling consumers to have sufficient purchasing power to fulfil their requirements. Production exists, needs exist, but there is a lack of finance and the Creditistes want to make it available to the consumer.
I refer to an article which appeared last February 19 in La Patrie, a newspaper which is well known for its Liberal sympathy. The article, which is to be found on page 10, was written by Claude Lavergne and is accompanied by a picture showing what is going on in the metropolis of Canada. Here is the heading of the article:

The poverty-stricken people cry for help hut nobody hears them.. .Deprived of the soup kitchen and the shelter, all they can do now is wait.
The tramps and poor people of Montreal are definitely not in a period of luck. They were hit hard when the Meurling shelter was closed down, that place of refuge where the homeless were housed every night. Then came another crusher: the closing down of the soup kitchen. And now the authorities are slow in helping distressed families. So much so that one might wonder if people are not deliberately blind to misery in the metropolis.
People act exactly as if those who suffer, those who are hungry and those who are cold were able to indulge in the luxury of waiting-
As for immediate assistance, such as the "shelter" or the "soup kitchen", it seems that they are gone forever, they are things of the past.
Relief granted to families under the law by social welfare still exists but things there are going so slowly that one can question its efficiency.
And the author goes on to say:
Since then, tramps wander from one parish to another, in search of a hunk of bread, but everyone passes the buck-
Passing the buck is a well-known thing.
-on the pretext of not having the financial means and the responsibility to give assistance to passers-by.
These relief institutions being closed down, the unfortunate are merely left to their fate. They have been thrown in the gutter.
And those destitute people are consumers who are entitled to live and enjoy a minimum standard of living, more particularly in a rich country like ours, which has only 18 million people but could easily yield a living for 100 million.
Those paupers have no money, no shelter, they lack clothing, housing, and the Liberal party helped them get some accommodation in 1963 by imposing an 11 per cent tax on building materials. Those poverty stricken people are, however, entitled to a vital minimum, they all have a right to live.
Why not give those poverty stricken people a national dividend based on mechanized production, on automation, which brought about such distress for the workers which it replaced.
Machines and automation will continue pauperizing people day by day, because every day technical progress of various kinds replaces the labour of man, and in our present system, when machines put people out of jobs, paupers are mass produced.
Automation means mass production. On the other hand, it produces pauperism, indigence, and a great number of people who lack security. Why? Because we progressed in every field, but we failed to adopt a financial system in harmony and in accordance with automation and mechanized production.
The practical solution for the individual would be this:

First, place the Bank of Canada at the service of the parliament of Canada.
Second, let the Canadian parliament use the money of the Bank of Canada, the money of its own bank, to provide, for each citizen, a national dividend based on production resulting from machinery, automation and mechanization.
Third, increase family allowances according to the cost of living index, using not borrowed money but the money of the Bank of Canada.
In actual fact, for public bodies, the solution would be the following:
First, put at the service of the provinces the necessary credit (interest-free) allowing them to develop without having to borrow in the United States or in other countries of the world.
Second, place at the disposal of municipalities and school boards a municipal development bank, which would be a branch of the Bank of Canada. This bank would supply the necessary credit allowing municipalities and school boards to have interest-free money to build schools, sidewalks, water and sewage systems and to pursue other public capital expenditures.
Why should a municipality, a school board pay $300,000 as principal and interest for a school when the construction thereof amounts to $100,000? By building a school worth $100,000 and making the citizens pay $300,000 for it, we defraud the local taxpayers by an amount of $200,000. This means, therefore, that the citizens of the community have obtained a school actually worth $100,000, and paid an additional $200,000 to the financial system, that is, one school for themselves and two schools for the financial system.
The unhappy fact with modern economists clinging to the old theories is that they do not make any difference between private and public capital.
Private capital is invested in private businesses to produce goods, and through the sale of those goods, private businesses make a profit which allows them to pay their loan interest. Social Crediters have always recognized that when money is loaned to produce goods and when it brings profit to one individual or to a group of individuals, it is normal that this individual or this group of individuals should pay interest on the amounts borrowed.
But public capital is entirely different, and the economists do not seem to know that. When a municipality invests $100,000 in the building of sidewalks in 1964, and when that same municipality will have to pay $300,000 25 years later, that is in 1989, for these side-
The Address-Mr. Rondeau walks, the difference between $100,000 and $300,000, that is $200,000, is stolen money.
Sidewalks are public utilities, they are public capital, they are public property; ten miles of sidewalks in 1964 will not make thirty miles of sidewalks in 1989. Now, if ten miles of sidewalks built in 1964 do not make thirty miles of sidewalks in 1989, why will the amount of $100,000 invested in those sidewalks in 1964 make a debt of $300,000 in 1989? If ten miles of sidewalks in 1964 cannot make 30 miles of sidewalks in 1989, why should the amount of $100,000 invested in those sidewalks in 1964 be repaid by an amount of $300,000 in 1989?
That is the explanation of all our public debt expansion. Buildings and improvements of a public capital nature are made for an amount of $1 and the public is being asked to repay $3. Therefore, the public is robbed of $2, because the federal government, the sole responsible for making capital available to public utility services, is paralysed by the very ones to whom it gave away its birthright for the mess of pottage of electoral funds.
The result of such an economic system is a crippling condition in every field.
We have a crippled farm policy, a crippled labour policy, a crippled industrial policy, a crippled municipal policy and a crippled school policy. Crippled by whom? By those who control finance.
Mackenzie King said in 1935:
Let me control money and credit in a country, and I shall not have to worry about those who make the laws.
Social Crediters want to see the end of the state of slavery imposed upon politicians by the controllers of finance. That is why they ask the federal government to use its own bank, the Bank of Canada, to put public capital at the service of the various public bodies, so that these bodies do not have to get $3 worth of public goods out of taxpayers who have obtained only $1 in real value.
The cancer of finance will eat away our public institutions, and our public bodies will in turn break up private enterprise if the federal government does not decide to take action and cut its tentacles.
If we want to get the Canadian economy moving, it is clear that after reforming our monetary system, we will have to cut taxes, grant a tax exemption of $2,500 to single persons and $5,000 to married persons, so that the Canadian consumers, through their purchasing power, can finance production.
Production must not be financed through debts payable in 30 years but must be disposed of today with today's money.

The Address-Mr. Rondeau
Our present system does the reverse: we buy yesterday's production with tomorrow's money, and then we wonder what is going wrong.
Money should be an exact accounting of our production.
Our national production should be considered as our national debit and money, as our national credit. The people create the debit by producing in quality and in quantity, and the government should see to it that our credit is at the disposal of our debit to have our production disposed of.
We are Social Crediters because we want our national credit to be controlled by the Canadian parliament, which could, through its accounting agency, the Bank of Canada, have our country's economy operating debt free, as opposed to what is taking place now.
The Social Crediters want the credit, or the money supply, of a nation to be the exact representation of its debit, and that debit is the production.
The old-line parties are debitists, that is to say they let our national production, which is our national debit, go to waste, destroy itself, lose itself in every way, through unemployment, for instance, because they do not control, in accounting terms, the credit column which would allow the debit column (production) to expend itself.
Social Crediters want to place credit and money at the service of production, the Canadian credit at the service of the Canadian debit, the Canadian production.
And the old debit parties leave production, our debit, go to waste for lack of credit, money.
Social Credit means credit controlled by society, social credit controlled by the government through its bank, the Bank of Canada, so that it may give the people as much purchasing power as they produce.
The old debit parties, leave the control of credit in this country in the hands of financiers who are throttling private enterprise, farmers, workers and who keep social classes in misery, because they do not put in circulation the necessary money to dispose of the goods produced by the various social classes.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks about the administration of the federal government, or more exactly about the debates in this house.
I propose that the debates held here in the house be broadcast on radio or television; that could be done two hours a day, which would be enough to enable the Canadian people to see and hear for themselves the staggering amount of stupidities and the endless speeches which offer no solution to the ills of our economy.

If our electors knew how much time and money are lost and that in the end no solution is found, if our electors could see what takes place in the house and hear the speeches which are made here, they would be shocked and that would certainly not be to the advantage of the two old parties which have administered Canada since confederation in 1867.
Canada is one of the few countries in the world which have not amended their constitution over the last 50 years-old parties take their time; and we proclaim that we are on the road to success.
We must amend our constitution, but we must repatriate it before we amend it; for it still rests in the hands of our mother-in-law, England. The Canadian daughter is not yet old enough to take care of her own business, according to the old parties.
We must repatriate our constitution, amend it and also our confederative pact of 1867. I do not believe that we shall be able to recapture the time lost since 1867 if we do not make better speed than the two old parties which have only two speeds: slow and stop.
We need a flag and a national anthem, and they should not be imported from abroad, but must be typically Canadian.
The time for speeches has lasted too long, since 1867. It is now time for action and for achievements before 1967, otherwise Canada will bring about its own downfall. The Creditistes will not be to blame; the responsibility will have to be shared entirely by the two old parties which, since confederation, have indulged in political sleep-walking and have given us as heritage the atmosphere of 1964, that is, a country threatened with the dislocation of the provinces, victims of the federal cancer.
The union of the two nations, in 1867, is on the verge of collapse and the problem will have to be settled, not by one party trying to fool the other, but through earnest and sincere efforts by everyone to make his share of sacrifices in order to prevent a national divorce, which would prove to the whole world that the two finest nations and the two most beautiful cultures on earth joined under the same skies in Canada have been unable to understand each other and to live on good terms in the most beautiful country on earth.
Will 1967 give the world the evidence of our incompatibility or will it be the beginning of a new harmonious existence between the two greatest cultures, the two finest races and languages united under the most beautiful skies of the world, Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I referred a few minutes ago to the 11 per cent tax and I would like to

introduce an amendment to the amendment of the Conservative party.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Megan tic (Mr. Langlois):
That the words "11 per cent" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
In order to replace it by an adjustment in family allowances according to the cost of living index.

Before the six o'clock recess, the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) moved the following amendment:
That the words after "11 per cent sales tax" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"in order to replace it by an adjusment in family allowances according to the cost of living index."
If we relate this amendment to the subject presently under discussion, the proposal would read as follows:
But we respectfully regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to propose the repeal of the 11 per cent sales tax in order to replace it by an adjustment in family allowances according to the cost of living index.
In my opinion, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Shefford is essentially the same as the one moved yesterday in this house by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). Though both amendments are drafted differently, they make the same proposal, that is the adjustment or the increase of family allowances proportionate to the cost of living index. This new proposal does not seem to be relevant to the main amendment; it endeavours to introduce an altogether new matter.
Moreover, the new proposal, despite the use of the words "in order to" which comes before, has no logical connection with the proposal it is supposed to amend. The amendment suggests the withdrawal of a tax in order to increase certain disbursements of the state, or else to reduce the revenue of the state in order to increase expenditures.
In this way the proposal is contrary to usage which requires an amendment to an amendment shall be drafted in such a way that, if it is accepted, the proposal so amended remains understandable and logical.
For those reasons, and by virtue of the authorities quoted by the Chair when rejecting the two subamendments proposed by the hon. members for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) and Beauce (Mr. Perron), I am sorry that I have to conclude that the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Shefford is out of order.

If time permits when I have concluded my speech I will be pleased to deal with any question he may raise. All of us recall that the present official opposition continued in office for six years, during most of which time it enjoyed an overwhelming majority in the house. Yet no effective steps were taken to tackle the problem of huge recurring deficits. I would hope, Mr. Speaker, if the present government remains in office four years, that by the end of that time not only would the federal deficit disappear but it would be possible either to reduce the national debt through surpluses or to consider tax reductions. I would hope that such reductions would be in the income taxes of the average working man where they are most needed.
When the sales tax was expanded to include building materials and machinery and apparatus last year, the Minister of Finance pointed out that a tax increase was essential from the point of view of national financial responsibility and that several alternatives were considered. These alternatives included (a) a 4 per cent increase in the existing sales tax or (b) a 20 per cent to 25 per cent increase in personal income tax or (c) a 10 per cent increase in corporate income tax.
The right hon. Leader of the Opposition has not proposed that any of these alternatives be pursued, nor does he propose any new solution. If the right hon. gentleman has found the magic formula for solving Canada's financial problems without pain, I am sure everyone in the house would welcome his outlining it to us. Indeed in this matter, as in so many others, he offers no alternative in his speech but instead proposes that this house be entirely irresponsible in fiscal matters. In his amendment the Leader of the Opposition states that this tax is "detrimental to various segments of the economy". He does not support this with any facts and figures, but rather relies on quotations from such interested parties as the Canadian Construction Association and the Canadian Lumbermen's Association.

speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, who does like taxes? No, Mr. Speaker; he is not speaking for the families who pay taxes on necessities. He is speaking for the large contractors, the large corporations and the special interests which this tax affects. In other words in this matter he is acting as the spokesman for the construction lobby which, in spite of an impending boom, got itself so well organized and brought such tremendous pressure upon members of the house that it was generally recognized last year that it was the best organized lobby in Canadian political history. This same pressure group was not satisfied with the concession that was made and is now saying, through the Leader of the Opposition, "Let us force a general election, and regardless of the welfare of Canadians generally we will get rid of these taxes which affect our particular interests". Last year, Mr. Speaker, when the sales tax exemption was lifted-

I accept responsibility for everything that I am saying, and I am also my own author.
Last year when the sales tax exemption was lifted it was widely stated that there would be a great slump in the construction industry. Government spokesmen pointed out that forecast did not bear out this pessimism. I am happy to say that 1963 proved to be a boom year. Construction improved in almost all categories, and the increase in winter built homes, due largely to the $500 government subsidy plan, has astounded even the severest critics of the government.
I maintain, as I did last fall, that the tax on production equipment and apparatus, when taken along with the incentives granted industry, has not materially affected production costs in this country. Indeed, Mr. George F. Plummer of Dunlop Canada Limited, who recently appeared before the Carter commission with a delegation representing the rubber association of Canada, correctly stated the case when he said that the sales tax on production machinery represented such a very small part of the over-all costs that it would

be unrealistic to claim this tax made a big difference in the cost of goods.
Let us look ahead. What are the 1964 prospects for the construction industry, now demanding a tax reduction, which would have to be made at the expense of all other Canadians? I quote from the February 22 edition of the Financial Post, page 49, where it is stated:
Canada's construction Industry is in for another good year in 1964, with over-all volume of business possibly reaching a record level of $8,000 million compared with an estimated $7,700 million in 1963.
I should like to refer to the same edition of the Financial Post to ascertain the position regionally with regard to the construction industry. On page 50 of the same paper, in respect of construction in Ontario, this newspaper says:
-the past president of the Toronto real estate board, R. W. Telford, has this to say. "There'li be a 3 per cent to 4 per cent increase in housing starts in 1964 compared with 1963". There were 148,600 starts last year compared with 130,029 in 1962.
This is an increase of some 18,600 houses. Let us look in the same edition of the Financial Post at the position of British Columbia. I quote from page 61:
Near record capital spending keeps business at a high level. Despite a slackening off in highway and bridge construction officials predict that the record level will continue through 1964 and may perhaps go even higher.
Let us move on to Alberta. On page 61 of the Financial Post I read:
Swelled by an estimated 12 per cent rise in industrial, commercial, institutional and engineering construction activity, Alberta's building industry became a billion dollar business in 1963. According to key indicators, 1964 promises an even greater percentage increase with over-all value of the industry reaching $1,200 million.
Let us look at Saskatchewan. On page 62 of the same issue of the Financial Post it is suggested that Saskatchewan's construction industry shows no signs of approaching a trough after recording a record year in 1963. New capital construction in 1963 totalled $344 million compared with $322 million in 1962, and the forecast for 1964 is $360 million.
Let us move on to Quebec. On page 63 of the same issue of the Financial Post it is stated that some of the biggest ever construction projects are under way in Quebec this year.
In so far as the maritimes are concerned, Mr. Speaker, page 63 of that newspaper suggests in respect of Nova Scotia that the value of contracts awarded in 1963 was $86.1 million, up nearly 15 per cent from 1962.
This is the picture across the whole country, Mr. Speaker, and I could supply similar quotations for every province. The construction
The Address-Mr. L. Watson industry is booming, and it will continue to thrive across the whole country next year. The quotations I have read were compiled by persons who know the industry and were reported in Canada's largest and most responsible financial newspaper. Yet, Mr. Speaker, we have before us today an amendment proposed by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition suggesting that the sales tax on building materials should be removed. These products, he says, should be exempted, with the inevitable result that either the taxes on personal incomes or on necessities such as clothing and household appliances would have to be increased or the government's deficit increased still further in the forthcoming year.
I believe this amendment, which would aid the few at the expense of the many, should be rejected as financially unsound. The one thing that pleases me about the amendment is that it was not seconded by the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings.

speechtext:
I should like to add my congratulations to those of other speakers to the mover and seconder of the address in reply. During the past year I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speeches of many members from many parts of this great Canada of ours. They referred, I believe, to every problem to which reference could be made in our various constituencies. I realize that many members from the same party have different ideas. This, I believe, is the proper way to bring out the best ideas from all across the Dominion of Canada.
Last year I enjoyed the descriptions of the various constituencies as each member gave a brief outline of his own riding and its problems. I am not going to follow this practice tonight, since I am sure that the name Assiniboia does not need any introduction in this House of Commons, but I will say it is one of the great agricultural areas of the province of Saskatchewan.
Since I am a farmer myself, I naturally wish to discuss some of the problems facing agriculture. The Saskatchewan farmer is a progressive man if given a chance. He knows exactly where he is heading. There is one thing which continuously plagues us in the west, and it is the uncertainty of the weather. Last year and again this year I listened with great interest to the speech from the throne. Think of the great promises which have been made. It was in my riding that the promise of $2 wheat was made at a time when wheat was already fetching $2 a bushel. This is where the promise of $3 wheat for a specified number of bushels was first heard. It was the hope of some people that one of the two

The Address-Mr. L. Watson ministers of agriculture might come from that constituency.
One of our problems has always been the storage of grain on the farm. This is a very serious matter. Most people do not realize that when the west has a good crop it must all be stored on the farms since the country and terminal elevators are usually filled at harvest time by the carryover from the crop of the previous year. The farmer is unfairly placed in the position of having to supply all this storage space to accommodate between 900 million and 950 million bushels of wheat, it is estimated, at peak periods. On the other hand, the grain companies can build elevators and annexes to a capacity of 700 million bushels, and as soon as the farmers deliver their grain the companies can begin to collect storage payments as well as write off their investment in depreciation.
I intend to suggest that the government should give considerable thought to making payments to farmers for the storage of grain on the farms. I know that arguments can be advanced' both for and against this proposition. I remember back in the election campaign of 1957 asking the Liberal candidate where he stood on this question. He gave all kinds of reasons why such payments could not possibly be made. He was not elected. However, in the 1958 election campaign he came back to the same hall and on this occasion he said "If you vote for me you will find we are in favour of making storage payments for farm stored grain". That was a complete reversal of his stand in 1957. The people of Saskatchewan realized that it was another political promise and treated it as such.
Another suggestion is this, that the rate of depreciation should be increased from the present rate of 5 per cent to 20 per cent on any building built on the farm to store grain. This would give the producer a chance to recover his money within a reasonable period of time, since these buildings are of no use when empty. This plan would not cost the government any money in payments. On the other hand it would bring in a great deal of revenue to the federal treasury through the collection of this 11 per cent tax monster with which we have to deal at the present time whenever we buy building supplies. We in the farming industry are not like those who can stockpile building material for future use. The time when we gather a crop is the time we have to buy in order to enlarge our storage facilities. It is only then that we can do some repairs and renovations to other buildings.
I should like to remind hon. members that it was the Conservative government which

got rid of the wheat surplus through the efforts of my hon. friend the member for Qu'Appelle and his aggressive plans for selling grain in world markets. We in Saskatchewan have been fortunate in harvesting good crops in 1962 and 1963 due to ideal moisture conditions. But, contrary to what the public believes, the grain situation is not good. More than 50 per cent of the delivery points are still on three and four bushel quotas. The Department of Trade and Commerce still has a big job to do on the 1963 crop, and it must be the responsibility of this government to get out and look for new markets in the future since the west is capable of producing even more grain, and will do so as, each year, more and more farmers become aware of the advantages of fertilizing and modern farming practice.
It was the Conservative government which showed the Liberals how to sell wheat. The attitude of the former government was very different from the attitude taken by the previous Liberal administration, which felt that if the customers wanted the wheat they could come and get it.
The cattle market all across Canada is declining. The price of choice steers at Calgary declined between December 1962 and December 1963 from $25.98 to $20.98 per cwt. Prices on the Toronto market have also fallen from $28.27 to $23.74 in the same period of time. This means that the decline in cattle prices at Toronto between December 1962 and December 1963 amounted to 16 per cent. In the same period of time, between January 1963 and January 1964, the fall in prices amounted to 11 per cent. Cattle exports in Canada have declined by 44 per cent since 1962, according to the dominion bureau of statistics. I could give hon. members the figures but I will not do so at this time.
It would not be fair to the new Minister of Transport not to mention rail line abandonment. The former minister, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mellraith), spent some time as a guest in the Assiniboia constituency a couple of weeks ago. I do not know whether it was as a result of this visit or not, but I noticed in the paper that it was the intention of the government to put the matter of rail line abandonment under the jurisdiction of the Department of Agriculture. This I do not understand. After all, who should know the railway problem better than the Minister of Transport? I appreciate, of course, that the problems involved are altogether different from those he encountered in his former post, and that they could be just as difficult.
This matter of rail line abandonment is a major problem in the west. I suggest that no rails should ever be lifted. If a line is not

paying-and I realize there could be many in this category, the way the railways operate -then regular runs might possibly be discontinued. As a last resort they should be maintained to haul grain, because the only sensible and economic way of transporting grain in Canada is by rail. The 5,220 elevators along these lines which helped to open up the west are just as important today, in keeping it open, as they were 50 years ago. The railway companies must realize that we produced approximately 550 million bushels of wheat in 1962, and that the 1963 crop of 723 million bushels is theirs to haul, with no competition from any quarter whatsoever since the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. are not in competition when it comes to gathering and hauling grain. They can threaten to remove the lines in the hope that the rates can be raised on grain so they can lower the rates on other commodities in order to compete against trucks, which can compete in other fields because the customers do get a more personalized and better service from trucking companies or individual truckers, who realize the need for service if they are to survive in the private enterprise field. This is quite different from the attitude of the railways.
As I mentioned before, Mr. Speaker, we will continue to produce grain, and' the government must look for new markets. This traffic is assured for the rail lines, which can surely find a means of handling it economically today, with large trains and modern facilities.
Mr. Speaker, I come from the province of Saskatchewan, where some may think we are indifferent to the bicultural problems in Canada. I would like to inform this house that I have in my riding 600 French families who do not speak English. I am not here to be concerned only with the problems of my own province; I am here to take an interest in the affairs of the whole country, regardless of these differences. I would like to read an article that appeared in the Regina Leader-Post of October 18, 1963, entitled "French Canadian Actors Speak Out". The article says, "West treats us like humans". This was a statement made by a group of French Canadian actors from Quebec. They went on to say, "The people of western Canada are open, friendly. They do not resist us because we are French Canadian. They treat us as humans".
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to leave with you the quotation "Be Canadians and the future is yours", which is credited to Louis Honore Frechette, member of parliament for Levis at that time. It appeared in a publication released by the Canadian
The Address-Mr. M. W. Martin speech from the throne on February 5, 1875, the hon. member's closing words were:
We will no longer be French, English, Scotch or Irish. We will be Canadians. We will form but one great nation with deep rooted patriotism and noble aspirations, working as one to common prosperity, and advancing together towards a great and productive future.
In my opinion these words apply as much today as they did in 1875. At this time, Mr. Speaker, I would also like to say that I feel it a great privilege and honour to be associated with all hon. members of all parties in the House of Commons.

For all the good that winter works program does in my part of the country I could vote against it very happily, because it is not designed in any way, shape or form to provide one hour's employment for the area I represent. I wonder whether there is any realization by this government of just what our unemployment problem is becoming; whether there is any realization that in certain skilled trades, and so on, there is a shortage of manpower in Canada today. We could employ many more people with skills; in fact skilled tradesmen are able to work all kinds of overtime. At the same time we have a large group of people who are rapidly approaching the stage of being practically unemployable in our society, and who are going to become permanent wards of the welfare system of this country unless this problem is tackled very rapidly and vigorously.
We see that some measures are to be brought in to deal with the railway problem, as they call it. But there is still no hint of the realization that we will not solve our transportation problems by putting a patch on the railway act, the highways act, the water act or some other act. If we are to tackle this problem properly we have to approach it as a universal Canadian railway transportation problem, and not put a patch here and there on the present rickety transportation problems.
Next we have an item dealing with minimum wages and maximum hours. Certainly

this is welcome. I think they should be a little shamefaced, after the 50 odd years they have governed the country out of the 97 years we have been in existence, that only now are they bringing in some measures in this field.
I think they are long overdue, and the government should hurry things up.
The next item mentions pensions, and what do we have? A very pale image of what was brought in last year. I wonder whether this government think, after being given a year of grace, that they are now going to be judged with great enthusiasm for bringing in a poor carbon copy of what they brought in last year and did not proceed with.
Then we have a very interesting item, Mr. Speaker. The government are going to embark on a project of student loans. Not only is this a poor substitute for the 10,000 scholarships which were promised so vigorously across the country, but I should like to examine for a moment what an empty facade this student loans business is. Surely it is a good and wonderful idea for students to be able to obtain loans interest free from the government until after they have completed their education and are able to go to work. But how many people are going to be able to take advantage of such loans? I do not know what the situation is across the country, but in the province of Ontario alone, according to the Ontario university presidents' report to the advisory committee on university affairs, at the present time our technological institutes have a capacity of 6,000 and have a need for a capacity of 18,000. Our universities, according to the report, are going to be about 6,000 short of that need in 1965, which is next year, and under present plans they will be from 20,000 to 30,000 short by 1970. I wonder how much good a loan will be to a student who has no university to which he can go. As I say, this is just an empty facade. It is making a big gesture which will not mean a single thing in meeting the problem in the educational field.
The next item, Mr. Speaker, makes some reference to legislation, or some measures to be brought in, in the field of housing. I hope these measures will bear some resemblance to the speeches which were made over the years by the Minister of National Revenue when he was the housing critic of the opposition. The minister is a very genial fellow, but I was wondering how long it is going to take him to influence the rest of the members of the cabinet and persuade them to go along with some of the ideas which he expressed when he was on this side of the house. We will not know until these measures are before us, but as I say I hope there are some better measures in this field than has been the case in the past.

Then we have a measure to deal with redistribution. That is an excellent thing; the only problem is it is about three years late. According to our constitution we are supposed to have a redistribution after every census, and I believe the last census was taken three years ago.
Then we have a measure which deals with Senate retirement. I believe there is some indication that the government are going to set an age limit of 75 years. I am wondering whether this is the type of Senate reform which is really going to be of benefit to the country, or whether it will just merely provide a few hiding places for politically embarrassing people.
Then we have a measure dealing with the equality of citizens' rights. Here again there seems to be a funny thing. We had the much heralded bill of rights passed here a few years ago, and as I mentioned before we have had 97 years of Liberal and Tory rule in this country. It seems rather strange that at this late date we have to bring in a measure to grant equality of rights to Canadian citizens.
These are not all the measures, Mr. Speaker. There are a few more which can be taken as measures, but I should like to deal briefly with some of the things which are not contained in the speech from the throne. One of them was mentioned the other day; in fact there was a vote in regard to it. I am referring to the glaring lack of any measure in the throne speech to provide medicare. Someone remarked to me the other day, Mr. Speaker, "One thing about you New Democrats in your fight for medicare; sometimes you have the Tories with you and sometimes you have the Liberals with you, but you never win a vote''. That seems to be the unhappy history of medicare in this house.
There is also no measure in the throne speech to bring family allowances up to what they should be if they are going to mean anything, or indeed to extend family allowances beyond the present age of 16. It seems rather strange that the government should talk, and not only talk but advertise the proposition extensively across the country, of urging people to remain at school, while at the same time cutting off their family allowance when they reach the age of 16. I have no children who have reached that age yet, but I am told by others who have that a child of 16, 17 or 18 years who is still going to school is just as expensive as one of 13, 14 or 15, if not more so. In fact, very recently when I brought the problem to the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare I received a reply from her which gave a very strong indication that that
The Address-Mr. M. W. Martin thought was in the mind of the government, in line with their previous commitments and promises, and that this particular matter should be dealt with and an extension made to family allowances as long as the child was still at school. However, such a proposal is missing.
There is no measure forecast in the throne speech to deal with the sad and sorry state of the unemployment insurance fund. Unfortunately I have seen some examples of what I believe are measures which this government has taken to tighten up this fund. However, if these measures are intended to cure the problems of the fund, I can assure the government that they are raising more problems than they are solving. Apparently the government have now embarked on a plan whereby they send out a form to applicants which consists of a group of questions which, in effect, are nothing more nor less than bear traps, as a result of which the unsuspecting automatically disqualify themselves. In fact I have had an admission from one of the staff at the local employment office, a quite frank and rather rueful admission, that the situation at present is that if a person who is a very good liar comes in he can qualify for unemployment insurance, but if a person comes in and tells the truth he is almost automatically disqualified.
There is no hint in the throne speech as to what this government plans to do to meet the problem of automation which is dislodging so many people across the country. There is nothing in this throne speech, Mr. Speaker, to deal with the exorbitant interest rates which are being charged across the country, eating away the purchasing power of the consumers like a cancer and becoming more and more prevalent and virulent every day. There is not a single measure, after the unhappy measures they embarked on last year, to deal with the problem of foreign ownership in this country.

Yes, another American bank, not to mention another Canadian brewery gone. There is nothing in the throne speech to deal with the problem of tax relief for the small income earner. The exemptions are left at the same amounts they were at some 10 or 15 years ago. I am not sure when the present exemptions of $1,000 per person and $2,000 per couple were put into effect, but it was a long time ago, and the cost of living and other expenses have risen by a great extent since then.
Last, but far from least, there is no mention in the throne speech of any corrective measure for one of the biggest mistakes made last
246	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. M. W. Martin session. Hon. members have been wondering just what I have here on my desk in this pile of documents, and whether they were notes for my speech that I intended to read into Hansard. I would point out these are just a few of the copies that came back in reply to sessional paper No. 108 of July 3, 1963, showing, and I quote, "Copies of all letters addressed to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance protesting the imposition of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials."
These were returned to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but being of a rather frail physique he was unable to transport them down to the chamber, so I volunteered to do it on his behalf. I have had no opportunity to read all of them; in fact I have not even had an opportunity to count them. I did weigh them, however, and they weigh somewhere in the neighbourhood of 100 pounds. They are a pretty good illustration that this amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition, contrary to what is said by some of my hon. friends on the left, was not a frivolous amendment. In fact I would say that this amendment did have a pretty solid base.
I have talked to many people in the construction industry since that ill fated measure was passed last year, introducing this tax. They tell me that it has created a state of confusion and chaos throughout the whole construction industry. They have never known from one day to the next just where they stood. One day there was an 11 per cent tax; the next day, it was removed. The following day they had a 4 per cent tax back on, with 4 per cent more to come on April 1 and 3 per cent more to come on January 1 of next year.
We have had a discourse by the hon. parliamentary secretary, talking about the great number of starts that have been made over the winter months. I imagine this was to try to show that that was a good measure which the government passed last year; but better reasons for the good number of starts were (1) we had a very mild winter; (2) the fact that they introduced a nice little gimmick, so that spending an extra $1,000 to build in winter you could get a bonus of $500; and (3) it was an out and out attempt to beat the tax which will be coming into effect on April 1.
There are no illusions in the minds of the people in this industry. One after another they have told me that the unexpected business they are getting now is nothing more or less than the business they would be getting in the spring, and it was merely transferred back from spring in order to avoid paying the extra 4 per cent tax.


My remarks tonight are brief, Mr. Speaker, but I think the country, and even this house, have given members of the government an opportunity to show what they are made of and what they intend to do to meet the problems of the country. If the throne speech they brought down two weeks ago is the best they can do, then I am afraid they certainly will not have much confidence across the country, and I do not think they should have the confidence of this house. We certainly intend to support the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition.
